It is estimated that approximately 50% of deaths in ICM are due to SCD [ 2 ] and CAD is the leading cause of malignant VA. Ventricular arrhythmias have also been associated with reduced quality of life and psychosocial symptoms, including depression and anxiety [ 3 ].

Based on current recommendations, patients with ICM receive implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICD) in the context of secondary VA prevention or for primary prevention when meeting certain criteria related to New York Heart Association (NYHA) class (NYHA II or more) and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤ 35% [ 4 , 5 ]. Nevertheless, despite their efficacy in treating VA and reducing death [ 6 ], ICDs do not prevent VA recurrences. Hence, almost one third of patients with ICD will experience VA within a few years from implantation [ 7 ]. In this context, catheter ablation (CA) and class III antiarrhythmic drugs (AAD) constitute first-line treatments to reduce recurrences [ 8 ]. Among class III AAD, amiodarone and sotalol are currently recommended in patients with structural heart disease, with amiodarone demonstrating a superior efficacy profile [ 9 ]. Regarding CA, the strongest evidence-based recommendation is for treating VA recurrences in patients on previous amiodarone treatment, whereas both amiodarone and CA are indicated in treatment-naïve patients [ 4 ].

Previous meta-analyses have been performed, though problems with poorly defined interventions and pooling of inhomogeneous interventions in the control group (beta-blockers and AAD) [ 10 ], significantly limit their clinical applicability. Furthermore, the VANISH-2 [ 11 ] and MANTRA-VT [ 12 ] trials were recently published comparing the efficacy and safety of CA versus Class III AAD, providing evidence in favor of CA in patients with ICM. Considering the above, the present systematic review (SR) and network meta-analysis (NMA) aimed to evaluate the comparative effectiveness and safety of CA versus class III AAD in the treatment of patients with ICM and ICD for secondary prevention by synthesizing updated evidence from available RCTs.

Methods The present study was conducted according to the guidance of Cochrane Handbook [ 13 ] and is pre-registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD42025640326). Amendments to the original protocol (accompanied by rationale) are reported in Table S.1 . Reporting was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [ 14 ] and its pertinent extension for NMA [ 15 ] (checklist in Table S.2). Ethical approval was not required due to the meta-analytical nature of the study.

Information sources and search strategy A systematic literature search was performed in MEDLINE (via Pubmed), Scopus and the Cochrane database from inception to October 26, 2025 (full search at Table S.3) without language restrictions. Supplemental searches were performed by citation chasing of included studies using the {citationchaser} R package and by manual search in ClinicalTrials.gov and Epistemonikos database.

Eligibility criteria Population, interventions, comparators, study design Patients with ICM having an ICD for secondary prevention of VA were included (patients with primary prevention were also analyzed only as a sensitivity analysis). Eligible interventions were CA and class III AADs (amiodarone, sotalol) being compared against each other or against standard care (SC). Only RCTs were eligible, having enrolled ≥ 70% ICM patients with a minimum follow-up duration ≥ 6 months. The 70% cut-off was used to ensure that the pooled studies predominantly represented ICM, while avoiding unnecessary exclusion of relevant trials to maintain statistical power and generalizability. A sensitivity analysis including only studies with 100% ICM patients was also performed.

Outcomes The primary efficacy outcomes were appropriate shock and electrical storm (ES). Secondary efficacy outcomes included VA recurrence, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular (CV) mortality, heart failure (HF) exacerbation, undetected VT (VT below ICD detection limit), cardiac hospitalization, VA hospitalization and appropriate antitachycardia pacing (ATP). The primary safety outcome was any serious adverse event (AE), while secondary safety outcomes included cardiac perforation, pericardial effusion (requiring drainage), stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), major bleeding, myocardial infarction (MI), hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, pulmonary toxicity and liver toxicity. Based on standardized definitions, in VA recurrence, episodes of appropriate ICD therapy (shock or ATP) or sustained (≥ 30s) VT/VF were included, while for ES, three or more VA episodes within 24h were eligible [ 16 ]. More detailed outcome definitions were adopted as perindividual study criteria. The definitions used for VA and AE in each study are presented in Table S.4, while detailed ICD programming (including zone cut-offs and treatments) in Table S.5. Data on analyzed outcomes were preferentially extracted from the intention-to-treat analyses.

Selection process Initially, titles and abstracts were screened by two authors independently. In this phase, studies were included for full text screening regardless of disagreements, to increase screening sensitivity. Subsequently, the same authors also independently evaluated the selected studies through full text screening. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or involvement of a third author. Abstrackr [ 17 ] and Mendeley Desktop were used.

Data extraction A draft extraction form was pilot-tested on three studies. After discussion and calibration exercises, a final extraction form was created. Extraction was performed independently by two authors and discrepancies were resolved through discussion or involvement of a third author. The approaches used to handle extraction issues were based on the Cochrane Handbook (Table S.6). Extracted variables are presented in Table S.7. To retrieve missing evidence, study protocols were reviewed.

Network geometry For the primary analysis, each network consisted of a maximum of three treatment nodes: CA, AAD and SC. Amiodarone and sotalol were merged under the category AAD. Standard care was considered the standard optimal medical treatment for patients with ICM, including revascularization, antiplatelets, hypolipidemic medication and HF treatment when indicated. As a secondary analysis, the node AAD was split into amiodarone and sotalol to further examine the comparative effectiveness and safety of interventions. This was feasible after a recent report from the VANISH-2 study [ 18 ] that reported outcomes separately for amiodarone and sotalol and under the reasonable assumption that both the SURVIVE-VT [ 19 ] (amiodarone 86%/sotalol 14%) and MANTRA-VT [ 12 ] trials (amiodarone 93%/sotalol 7%) were analyzed as amiodarone-only studies. This ancillary analysis was performed to provide further insights into the comparative effectiveness of CA against different AAD and to aid in the interpretation of the main analysis.

Risk of bias assessments Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias (RoB) of included studies (at the study level) using all the prespecified domains of the revised version of the Cochrane Collaboration tool (RoB 2) [ 20 ]. Disagreements were resolved upon discussion.

Data analysis All analyses were performed using R Statistical Software (v. 4.4.2) and the package ‘netmeta’ [ 21 ]. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies with percentages (%), while continuous variables are presented as mean with standard deviation (SD) when normally distributed, otherwise as median with interquartile range (IQR). To estimate differences between interventions, the risk ratio (RR) was used. Direct effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using the inverse variance weighting method for random-effects models. Direct and indirect estimates were combined using random-effects frequentist NMA models with the Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimator [ 22 ]. In case of zero events, a continuity correction of 0.5 was applied. Global network homogeneity was assessed with the Cochran’s Q test and between-study variance with the τ 2 . The I 2 metric was used to estimate between-study heterogeneity. Values of I 2 range between 0–100, with higher values indicating larger heterogeneity. Proposed interpretation cut-offs [ 13 ] are 0%-40%: might not be important; 30%-60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity; 50%-90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity; 75%-100%: considerable heterogeneity. A common heterogeneity measure was assumed for the whole network.

The transitivity assumption was evaluated qualitatively through the comparison of the distribution of potential effect modifiers across different treatments and comparisons (age, male percentage, percentage of patients with CAD, percentage of NYHA class I, LVEF, beta blocker usage). Statistical inconsistency was assessed locally through the node-splitting method [ 23 ] and globally through the design-by-treatment test [ 24 ]. The relative contribution of the direct and indirect effects on the overall network estimate for each outcome is presented with contribution plots. To rank interventions, the P-score was used [ 25 ], which takes values between 0–1 and reflects the certainty that a given intervention is superior to competing interventions, based on the estimates and standard errors of all pairwise comparisons in the network. A higher P-score indicates a higher probability that an intervention is among the most effective options, whereas lower values indicate poorer relative performance. Small study effect (including publication bias) was assessed visually with comparison-adjusted funnel plots and formally tested with the Egger’s test. For all statistical tests, a two-tailed p -value < 0.05 was considered significant.

Sensitivity analyses were performed for all outcomes based on: (i) the type of VA prevention (including both primary and secondary prevention patients), (ii) the percentage of ICM (including only studies with 100% ICM patients), (iii) the number of patients (including studies that enrolled ≥ 100 patients), iv) the implementation of HF treatment (including studies that started to enroll patients after 2000, where mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists had been introduced in HF management) and v) the implementation of less aggressive ICD therapies (including studies that started to enroll after the publication of MADIT-RIT trial [ 26 ]). Additional analyses including only patients with more pronounced systolic dysfunction (e.g. LVEF < 30%) or patients presenting with ES were not feasible due to incomplete reporting in analyzed trials.

Results Study selection and characteristics In total, 10259 records were screened, 10213 articles were excluded, and 46 articles were evaluated through full text screening. After the exclusion process (excluded studies with rationale in Table S.8), 14 RCTs (13 in the main analysis for secondary prevention only; 14 in sensitivity analysis for both primary and secondary prevention) and 2237 patients (2177 in main analysis) were analyzed (Figure S.1 ). Study characteristics and references of included RCTs are presented in Table 1 , population characteristics in Table S.9 and the procedural characteristics of each CA study (including arrhythmia-related inclusion criteria) in Table S.1 0. The distribution of potential effect modifiers across different treatment nodes stratified by each outcome is presented in Table S.1 1 and across different comparisons in Table S.1 2. The mean follow-up time was 24 (11) months, the mean age was 65.5 (3.2) years, the mean LVEF was 34.3% (2.8), the mean use of beta-blockers was 83%, 95% of patients had ICM, and publication year ranged between 1998–2025. Ten out of 14 (71%) studies used CA, 4/14 (29%) used amiodarone only, 4/14 (24%) used both amiodarone and sotalol (with greater proportional use of amiodarone compared to sotalol) and 3/14 (21%) used sotalol only. Studies’ overall RoB was evaluated as “Low” in 8/14 (57%) of trials, “Some concerns” in 4/14 (29%) and “High” in 2/14 (14%) of studies (Fig. 1 ; Table S.13 ). Efficacy outcomes Regarding appropriate shock (12 studies, 2154 participants; I 2 = 56%; p inconsistency = 0.249; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 A), CA ranked first with significant differences against AAD (RR = 0.68, 95%CI = [0.47, 0.99]; p = 0.043; P-score = 0.99), mainly driven by the comparison versus sotalol (RR = 0.42, 95%CI = [0.26,0.69]; Table S.1 6), with no difference versus amiodarone (RR = 0.91, 95%CI = [0.57,1.46]; Table S.1 6). In ES (8 studies; 1270 participants; I 2 = 26%; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 B), CA ranked first but was not superior against AAD (RR = 0.81, 95%CI = [0.63,1.03]; p = 0.088; P-score = 0.96). No evidence of small study effect was identified for any primary outcome (funnel plots in Figure S.3 ).

In VA recurrence (10 studies, 1208 participants; I 2 = 49%; p inconsistency = 0.119; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 C), no significant differences were found between CA and AAD (RR = 0.86, 95%CI = [0.68,1.08]; p = 0.197, P-score = 0.93). Regarding all-cause mortality, (13 studies, 2181 participants; I 2 = 0%; p inconsistency = 0.257; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 D), CA did not differ significantly from AAD (RR = 0.88, 95%CI = [0.70,1.12]; p = 0.316, P-score = 0.84). In CV mortality (5 studies, 977 participants; I 2 = 0%; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 E), CA was also not superior to AAD (RR = 1.04, 95%CI = [0.74,1.47]; p = 0.828, P-score = 0.63). Regarding HF exacerbation (10 studies, 1893 participants; I 2 = 0%; p inconsistency = 0.136; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 F), CA was superior to AAD (RR = 0.76, 95%CI = [0.58,0.99]; p = 0.043, P-score = 0.82), mainly due to the comparison versus amiodarone (RR = 0.67, 95%CI = [0.41,1.11]; Table S.1 6) and less so against sotalol (RR = 0.82, 95%CI = [0.43,1.55]; Table S.1 6).

Concerning the outcome of undetected VT-below ICD detection limit (3 studies, 819 participants; I 2 = 0%; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 G), CA ranked first and was superior to AAD (RR = 0.27, 95%CI = [0.15,0.46]; p < 0.001, P-score = 1) both against amiodarone (RR = 0.27, 95%CI = [0.15,0.49]; Table S.1 7) and sotalol (RR = 0.25, 95%CI = [0.13,0.49]; Table S.1 7). Of note, all three studies contributing to undetected VT (SURVIVE-VT, VANISH, VANISH-2) had programmed a VT-1 therapy zone ranging from 15–20 bpm lower than the slowest documented VT to a minimum of 130–150 bpm coupled with ATP therapies. Regarding hospitalization for cardiac causes (4 studies, 926 participants; I 2 = 57%; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 H), CA did not differ against AAD (RR = 0.79, 95%CI = [0.57,1.09]; p = 0.156; P-score = 0.93). In VA hospitalization (3 studies, 229 participants; I 2 = 66%; Table 2 ; F i g. 3 I), CA was not superior against AAD (RR = 0.66, 95%CI = [0.22,1.98]; p = 0.453, P-score = 0.77), while also no significant differences were found in appropriate ATP reduction (6 studies, 1024 participants; I 2 = 29%; p inconsistency = 0.454; Table 2 ) between these interventions (RR = 0.96, 95%CI = [0.85,1.10]; p = 0.573, P-score = 0.74).

Safety outcomes Regarding the primary safety outcome of any serious AE (4 studies, 698 participants; I 2 = 63%; Table 2 ; Fig. 4 A) no difference was identified between CA and AAD (RR = 0.63, 95%CI = [0.33,1.23]; p = 0.176, P-score = 0.67) in the primary analysis. In the secondary analysis, CA was superior to amiodarone (RR = 0.33, 95%CI = [0.15,0.75]; Table S.1 6) and neutral against sotalol (RR = 0.39, 95%CI = [0.12,1.32]; Table S.1 6). For all the rest CA-related safety outcomes, an increased but nonsignificant risk was found for CA versus AAD in cardiac perforation, pericardial effusion requiring drainage, stroke/TIA, major bleeding and MI (Fig. 4 ). Regarding the AAD-related safety events, CA was associated with a smaller risk of hyperthyroidism (RR = 0.40, 95%CI = [0.17,0.92]; p = 0.031, P-score = 0.74) and pulmonary toxicity (RR = 0.28, 95%CI = [0.09,0.92]; p = 0.036, P-score = 0.60), driven by the comparison against amiodarone (Table S.1 6). Marginally nonsignificant differences were found in hypothyroidism and liver toxicity (Fig. 4 G and J respectively).

Sensitivity analyses The results of the sensitivity analyses are shown in Figures S.25 - S.34 . In general, no noteworthy differences were observed regarding either the ranking of interventions or the magnitude and the direction effect estimates in all efficacy and safety outcomes. A table summarizing the exact studies that were analyzed in the main and sensitivity analyses is presented in Table S.1 7.

Discussion Summary of findings in the context of other evidence This is the first NMA to summarize the existing evidence by appropriately analyzing each individual intervention separately. Previous meta-analyses for VT ablation in ICM have provided effect estimates of CA versus control groups that comprised both AAD and SC into one group [ 10 , 37 , 38 ]. In contrast to this, using a NMA methodology, we split SC from AAD in our primary analysis, and we separately analyzed amiodarone and sotalol in our secondary analysis rendering our results clinically relevant and interpretable. In short, the findings of our main analysis suggest that in patients with ICM and ICD for secondary VA prevention, CA is superior to AAD in terms of efficacy with comparable safety. Indeed, CA was superior to AAD in reducing appropriate shocks, undetected VT and HF exacerbation. The effect on appropriate shocks was mainly versus sotalol, while in HF, versus amiodarone. The superiority in undetected VT was consistent against both amiodarone and sotalol.

Ablation was associated with a 19% reduction in ES and a 14% reduction in VA recurrence, though both effects were nonsignificant. It is possible, however, that patients presenting with ES might benefit more from CA as compared to patients with at least one documented VA (which was our inclusion criterion) based on the results of a recently published meta-analysis [ 39 ]. The neutral effect on total VA recurrences may be partly explained by the neutral effect on appropriate ATP reduction, which accounted for a larger proportion of appropriate ICD therapies compared to shocks (47% vs 33%) in our study. Interestingly, the reductions in appropriate shocks and undetected VT are directly associated with the benefits in HF exacerbation. Shocks, even when appropriate, do cause myocardial stunning, often leading to hospitalization and cardiac decompensation while worsening prognosis [ 40 , 41 ]. Finally, undetected VT – often associated with extensive fibrosis and scar-related reentry circuits with multiple exits [ 42 ], as well as AAD treatment [ 43 ]– may turn into VF or lead to cardiac decompensation, itself a trigger for VAs, leading to a vicious cycle.

In our analysis, CA did not significantly impact all-cause or cardiovascular mortality. This finding aligns with previous evidence indicating that recurrent VA—whose incidence was not significantly reduced by ablation—remains a major determinant of adverse prognosis. In VANISH and VANISH-2 trials-which constitute the largest RCTs in the field-the significant effect on the primary composite endpoints were mainly driven by other co-primary endpoints and not from all-cause mortality. Similar results have been reported in the PAUSE-SCD trial that included patients with ischemic and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. In this study ablation efficacy was driven by arrhythmia reduction rather than CV hospitalization or mortality [ 44 ]. This observation might be partly explained by reductions already achieved through optimal medical and interventional therapy [ 45 ]. The timing of CA could also serve as a significant effect modifier. Indeed, the recently published PREVENTIVE-VT trial [ 33 ] demonstrated considerable efficacy of CA in the primary prevention of arrhythmias, reducing not only arrhythmia-related, but also major clinical outcomes. Accordingly, in 528 patients treated with CA, age, NYHA class and ES were independent predictors of cardiac mortality after VT ablation [ 46 ], while based on the PAINESD score [ 47 ], age, NYHA class and LVEF constitute predictors of hemodynamic decompensation. Collectively, these data mandate for early intervention.

Regarding AEs, it is noteworthy that VT ablation (despite its complexity and application in morbid patients) demonstrated comparable safety against AAD in several treatment-related and serious AE, including stroke, need for pericardiocentesis, vascular complications and major bleeding. Interestingly, it was also superior against amiodarone regarding serious AE, while amiodarone was also associated with a higher risk of hyperthyroidism and pulmonary toxicity. Despite an overall rate of complications exceeding 13% [ 48 , 49 ], temporal trends in major complications appear to remain stable ranging between 4%-8% [ 48 , 50 , 51 ]. Most frequent complications are associated with vascular access site (58% of major complications) [ 50 ], while other complications (including cardiac tamponade) appear to rise sharply when epicardial procedures are also included [ 48 ]. However, recent advancements have significantly improved the safety of epicardial access for VT ablation. Among them, the carbon dioxide (CO₂) insufflation technique, as described by Santangeli et al. [ 52 ], represents a major procedural innovation. In this approach, intrapericardial CO2 insufflation creates a pericardial separation that facilitates needle entry, minimizing myocardial or coronary injury, and inadvertent entry into adjacent structures.

Factors associated with major complications include [ 48 , 50 , 51 ]: structural heart disease (especially ICM), ES, non-elective procedures, and biventricular access. Mortality in the early post-ablation period (in-hospital and 30-day) ranges from 5% in older cohorts to 1.8% in newer studies, is mostly associated with arrhythmia recurrence (44.5%-80%) [ 48 , 51 ] and is further increased when bail-out mechanical circulatory support is implemented (up to 88% within 10 days) [ 53 ]. Conversely, prophylactic circulatory support was associated with 33% reduced death/transplantation rates at 12 months post-ablation [ 54 ]. The Risk In Vt Ablation (RIVA) score may predict major complications and in-hospital mortality, with estimates ranging from < 5% to > 50% [ 48 ]. The positive association between operator’s experience and procedural safety should also be accounted in complex VT ablation procedures [ 55 ].

It is noteworthy that our results could have underestimated the effectiveness of CA. Class III AAD have been compared against SC in older trials where background therapy for HF and revascularization techniques were inferior, thus their additional effect on outcomes was more pronounced. Moreover, despite pharmacological stagnation over the 27-year span from the first included study (1998–2025), CA has shown significant advancements [ 56 ]. A paradigm shift has been observed from activation mapping to substrate modification with improved outcomes for patients with structural heart disease [ 57 ]. However, substrate ablation, when performed at all, was not based on high-density mapping and was limited to potential channel identification and pace-based mapping confirmation. A more modern elaboration of this approach is functional substrate mapping, where potential critical points for ablation are identified based on electrogram properties. Most variations are based on late potentials and local abnormal ventricular activities (LAVA) abolition (including potentials evoked during rapid pacing – decrement-evoked potentials – DeEP approach) and on ablating perpendicular to wavefront propagation in areas with isochronal confluence (isochronal latest activation mapping – ILAM) [ 58 , 59 ]. Moreover, the introduction of high-density mapping and the notion of omnipolar potentials using grid catheters allows for better discrimination between near- and far-field signals and improved determination of wavefront propagation, facilitating the identification of conduction channels and VT exit sites [ 60 ]. To summarize, this technology dependence must be considered when evaluating the findings of our meta-analysis, where older studies may no longer reflect current practice outcomes due to the use of outdated technology.

Implications for practice and research The present NMA suggests that CA has superior efficacy with similar safety compared to AADs, which is particularly relevant in the era of prolonged survival of ICM patients with need for long-term VA suppression. The same applies in ES, justifying the ESC 2015 recommendations granting CA a first-line treatment status in dedicated centers [ 61 ]. Current guidelines recommend the use of catheter ablation in preference to escalating AAD therapy in patients with CAD and recurrent sustained VT despite amiodarone therapy. This recommendation stems mainly from the VANISH trial where a strategy of escalating antiarrhythmic medications was inferior to CA. Nevertheless, CA is not prioritized in patients solely on beta-blocker compared to AAD. Based on our results, the use of first-line CA over AAD in these patients seems reasonable, more so if there is a history or strong suspicion for VT below ICD detection threshold. Moreover, the reductions in HF exacerbation associated with CA merit particular attention. Even though HF was not a targeted outcome for most of the included studies, the robustness of our analysis and the lack of heterogeneity or inconsistency in this outcome increase the strength of our conclusions. Hence, the effect of CA on HF merits further consideration in future studies.

Recently published studies have highlighted the time-dependent efficacy of CA. A meta-analysis of seven RCT suggested that early CA was more beneficial compared to a deferred strategy [ 62 ]. In an even more revolutionary approach, the PREVENTIVE-VT trial demonstrated a significant benefit of CA for primary prevention in patients with ICM and chronic total coronary occlusions [ 33 ]. Hence, future research should focus on the effectiveness and safety of prophylactic CA in the modern era. Accordingly, the awaited results of the CASTLE-VT trial [ 63 ], where prophylactic CA in patients referred for heart transplantation will be tested, as well as those of the PREVENT-VT ( NCT06543173 ) will shed more light on the field.

Further technological advancements may also improve outcomes for patients at risk for VA. A radical approach to CA lies in assessing the arrhythmogenic substrate using cardiac magnetic resonance [ 64 , 65 ] or computed tomography [ 66 ] and even perform noninvasive programmed ventricular stimulation, to determine critical isthmuses pre-procedurally and minimize lesion formation [ 58 , 67 ]. Additionally, the advent of digital twins could further facilitate the identification of the active part of a VT circuit [ 68 ]. Positive experience is also increasing with the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms during the mapping procedure, suggesting the optimal ablation site [ 69 , 70 ]. Finally, the use of pulsed-field ablation (PFA) in the field of VA [ 71 – 74 ] is emerging, given its ability to target cardiomyocytes specifically and the potential for more clearly delineated, deep lesion formation. In this direction, the promising results of VT ablation using a lattice-tip PFA catheter provided the first evidence of feasibility and safety in the AVAAR registry [ 75 ].

Strengths and limitations In general, we have conducted a rigorous analysis adhering to pertinent methodological and reporting guidelines and to a pre-registered protocol. The analysis of AAD as one group coupled with the separate analysis for amiodarone and sotalol further reinforce the clinical applicability of our results. Moreover, heterogeneity was minimal and the transitivity assumption seemed plausible for all outcomes, since statistical inconsistency (when feasible to be evaluated) was nonsignificant. Furthermore, no differences were found in the qualitative examination of the transitivity assumption via the distribution of potential effect modifiers across interventions and comparisons. Additionally, our results remained relatively robust in sensitivity analyses, whereas only a minority of the analyzed studies were at “High” RoB. Collectively, these observations increase the validity of our study.

Nonetheless, some limitations should also be acknowledged. In certain outcomes we followed the per-study definitions, which may impact the generalizability of our results. Technological advancements in contemporary CA practice might have also been underrepresented in our study, possibly leading to underestimation of CA efficacy. Additionally, variations were encountered in the reporting of VA events across studies and ICD programming was not uniform. Moreover, our analysis only included RCTs, which, despite being the gold standard for causal inference, usually fail to adequately represent the wide spectrum of different scenarios encountered in clinical practice. Additionally, despite the pooling of all available data from RCTs, our analysis might have been underpowered to detect significant effects in outcomes that were underrepresented by primary studies. Finally, additional analyses focusing on certain subgroups (e.g. patients with very low LVEF or patients presenting with ES) were not feasible due to lack of separate outcome reporting in individual studies.

Conclusions In conclusion, based on our main analysis, CA is superior in terms of efficacy with similar safety compared to class III AAD in reducing appropriate shocks, VT below ICD detection limit and HF exacerbation in patients with ICM and an ICD for secondary VA prevention. No significant reductions were observed in VA or cardiac hospitalization and all-cause or CV mortality. Notably, in our secondary analyses CA demonstrated superior efficacy over sotalol and superior safety over amiodarone. Given the plausibility of the transitivity assumption and the robustness of our results in sensitivity analyses, the conclusions of our study seem valid. New RCTs incorporating novel advances in the field of CA, including mapping (functional substrate, omnipolar potentials, virtual mapping and use of AI) and energy type (PFA) are necessary to determine the true potential and advantages of VT ablation over pharmacotherapy.

ABSTRACT Background The optimal timing of catheter ablation for ventricular tachycardia (VT) in ischemic cardiomyopathy remains uncertain, with strategies ranging from prophylactic intervention to delayed treatment after recurrent arrhythmia. Increasing evidence suggests that the timing of ablation may critically influence both arrhythmic and clinical outcomes. Objective To synthesize contemporary evidence on VT ablation timing and to examine the mechanistic and clinical rationale supporting a timing‐oriented therapeutic framework.

Methods We performed a structured narrative review of randomized trials, observational studies, and mechanistic investigations evaluating different ablation strategies, including prophylactic, early, and ICD‐guided approaches. Particular emphasis was placed on integrating clinical outcomes with experimental and imaging data on post‐infarct substrate evolution.

Results Prophylactic ablation reduces arrhythmic burden but has not demonstrated consistent survival benefit. Early ablation strategies improve procedural outcomes but are limited by heterogeneous definitions and inconsistent prognostic impact. By contrast, a timely ICD‐guided approach—based on the first device‐verified arrhythmic event—has demonstrated consistent reductions in VT recurrence and ICD therapies, with emerging but heterogeneous signals of survival benefit in randomized trials. Mechanistic evidence supports this paradigm, showing that the post‐infarct scar is dynamic and continues to remodel over time, with increasing arrhythmogenic complexity. The first ICD‐treated arrhythmia may therefore represent a biologically meaningful inflection point for intervention. Imaging and computational tools can refine patient selection and procedural planning after this trigger, while emerging ablation technologies may expand treatment options but do not modify timing strategies.

Conclusions A timing‐oriented approach to VT ablation, anchored to clinically meaningful ICD‐verified arrhythmic events, provides the most coherent integration of mechanistic insight and clinical evidence. This strategy may also have relevant implications for healthcare utilization, although formal cost‐effectiveness data remain limited. Scar-related ventricular tachycardia (VT) is increasingly recognized as a three-dimensional (3D) arrhythmia sustained by complex reentrant circuits that frequently involve intramural components. Advances in high-density and high-resolution electroanatomical mapping have shifted the paradigm of substrate characterization from purely voltage-based structural definitions toward functional assessment of conduction delay and wavefront discontinuity. Recent studies have described techniques that target critical conduction abnormalities associated with VT circuits, including deceleration zones, lines of conduction block, and rotational activation patterns. A central concept underlying these approaches is that VT substrates are volumetric structures constrained by lateral and depth-oriented boundaries rather than planar pathways. Within this 3D framework, targeted ablation strategies that interrupt functionally relevant conduction abnormalities, rather than empirically modifying scar, have demonstrated clinical outcomes comparable to those of extensive homogenization approaches while potentially reducing procedural burden. Intramural reentry remains a major challenge because surface-based mapping incompletely captures mid-myocardial conduction, and current techniques for real-time intraprocedural assessment of intramural abnormalities remain limited. Adjunctive strategies, including differential pacing, refined annotation methods, and peak frequency analysis, may improve identification of critical substrate components, although no single parameter reliably defines the optimal ablation target. Accordingly, procedural endpoints should evolve beyond empirical surrogates such as VT termination or noninducibility toward confirmation of effective disruption of the 3D arrhythmogenic substrate. Introduction Scar-related ventricular tachycardia (VT) remains a major cause of lethal arrhythmias in patients with both ischemic and nonischemic cardiomyopathies, and catheter ablation has become an essential therapeutic option for cases refractory to antiarrhythmic drug therapy [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]. Despite substantial advances in mapping and ablation technologies, VT recurrence remains common, underscoring persistent limitations in our understanding of the arrhythmogenic substrate and in the definition of procedural success. Successful ablation requires accurate elucidation of the mechanisms sustaining reentry and appropriate selection of an ablation strategy tailored to the underlying substrate. Traditionally, induction of VT, mapping during tachycardia, termination by ablation, and subsequent noninducibility have been regarded as hallmarks of procedural success. However, because many scar-related VTs are hemodynamically unstable, substrate modification performed during sinus rhythm has evolved as the central strategy in VT ablation [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ].

Conventional substrate mapping has largely relied on a two-dimensional (2D) conceptual framework, focusing on the identification of low-voltage areas, late potentials, and fractionated electrograms. Despite these approaches, VT recurrence rates remain substantial, highlighting the need for a more fundamental understanding of the underlying reentrant circuit architecture. Advances in high-density and high-resolution mapping technologies have enabled more refined characterization of conduction delay, wavefront discontinuity, and critical isthmus regions during sinus or paced rhythm [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Furthermore, emerging evidence from high-density mapping and simultaneous endocardial–epicardial studies indicates that VT circuits frequently exhibit complex three-dimensional (3D) architectures involving subendocardial, intramural, and subepicardial components [ 15 ]. These observations challenge the traditional planar model of VT reentry and suggest that many apparent surface findings may represent projections of deeper volumetric circuits.

In parallel with this evolving understanding of 3D VT circuits, ablation strategies have progressively moved from empiric scar modification toward targeted approaches aimed at interrupting mechanistically defined critical conduction abnormalities. Nevertheless, important questions remain regarding how best to identify these abnormalities, how extensively ablation should be delivered, and how procedural success should be assessed when the arrhythmogenic substrate itself is 3D.

In this review, we integrate emerging insights into functional and 3D arrhythmogenic substrates with contemporary substrate-based ablation strategies and discuss how these concepts reshape both targeting strategies and procedural endpoints in scar-related VT ablation.

2. Classical Concepts of Scar-Related VT and Their Limitations VT reentrant circuits have been conventionally conceptualized as 2D structures composed of a narrow isthmus bordered by two electrically unexcitable barriers. This schematic representation has long served as the dominant framework for understanding VT mechanisms and has been clinically supported by findings from entrainment mapping studies [ 16 , 17 ]. With the introduction of 3D electroanatomical mapping systems, early ablation strategies focused on visualizing activation patterns on the endocardial surface using color-coded maps during VT, thereby identifying ablation targets based on tachycardia activation sequences [ 18 ]—an approach commonly referred to as a “VT activation-guided strategy”. However, as VT is often hemodynamically intolerable, substrate-based ablation during sinus rhythm or paced rhythm has become the predominant contemporary strategy.

Histopathological investigations of explanted human hearts have provided important insights into the structural basis of post-infarction VT. Surviving myocardial fibers may form interconnecting channels within the borders of fibrotic tissue and can function as slow-conducting pathways that support reentrant VT circuits [ 19 , 20 ]. Based on this understanding, surgical subendocardial resection targeting abnormal and fractionated electrograms demonstrated favorable long-term arrhythmia-free outcomes, with reported success rates of approximately 60–80% in patients with prior myocardial infarction [ 21 ]. These surgical experiences laid the conceptual foundation for catheter-based substrate ablation strategies, in which abnormal electrograms within scar tissue are identified and ablated [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ]. Electrically isolating the low-voltage scar segment that constitutes the core of the ventricular tachycardia substrate–with confirmation of exit block–represents an effective strategy rather than ablating the entire scar (Fig. 1 ).

Bipolar voltage mapping has been widely adopted to delineate dense scar and the scar border zone. Nevertheless, there are several important limitations of voltage-based scar definition. Bipolar voltage amplitude is highly dependent on electrode size, interelectrode spacing, and the direction of wavefront propagation, and it lacks the specificity required to distinguish arrhythmogenic scar from non-arrhythmogenic tissue [ 22 , 23 ]. Consequently, the simplistic assumption that low-voltage regions directly correspond to critical arrhythmogenic substrate has proven inadequate, contributing to the adoption of extensive scar homogenization approaches.

Late potentials and local abnormal ventricular activities (LAVA) depend on the recording site and the direction and sequence of activation during mapping [ 23 , 24 ]. These electrogram features may arise not only from components of the VT circuit but also from collision of activation wavefronts propagating from different directions, even at sites unrelated to the reentrant pathway [ 25 ]. As a result, reliance on late potentials alone has been shown to have limited specificity for identifying critical components of VT circuits. In addition, extensive scar homogenization represents a “probabilistically robust” strategy, in that widespread lesion delivery increases the likelihood of intersecting at least one critical component of a 3D reentrant circuit [ 10 ]. However, this approach entails significant procedural and clinical burdens, including increased lesion burden, prolonged procedural duration, potential adverse effects on ventricular function, and a potentially higher risk of complications.

Importantly, these limitations stem from a fundamental conceptual issue: voltage-based approaches primarily describe structural anatomy rather than the dynamic properties of conduction. Bipolar voltage amplitude reflects the presence of scar but does not directly characterize the spatial distribution of conduction delay, wavefront discontinuity, or functional barriers that sustain reentry. As a result, anatomical scar definition alone may incompletely identify the critical components of a VT circuit.

These considerations have prompted a paradigm shift from purely structural substrate mapping toward functional characterization of conduction dynamics, enabled by high-density and high-resolution mapping technologies.

3. High-Density/High-Resolution Mapping and Functional Substrate Advances in high-density and high-resolution mapping technologies have provided a new perspective for defining arrhythmogenic substrates based on functional properties, particularly conduction delay and conduction discontinuity [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. This paradigm shift—from purely structural substrate mapping toward functional substrate mapping—has drawn increasing attention as a strategy to identify myocardial regions more specifically associated with VT circuits. By focusing on electrophysiological characteristics rather than voltage amplitude alone, functional mapping aims to localize substrates that are more likely to represent critical components of reentrant tachycardia.

Irie, Tung, and colleagues [ 26 ] introduced Isochronal Late Activation Mapping (ILAM), a technique in which ventricular activation during sinus rhythm is temporally divided into eight equal isochronal segments to visualize localized conduction slowing as isochronal crowding. Using this approach, they demonstrated that regions of delayed activation can be clearly identified during sinus rhythm and that these regions may represent arrhythmogenic substrates independent of bipolar voltage amplitude [ 26 ]. Areas in which three or more isochrones were crowded within a distance of 1 cm were defined as deceleration zones (DZs) and were proposed as critical substrates identifiable during sinus rhythm [ 13 ]. DZs were present at 95% of sites where VT termination was achieved, and reproducibility of DZ location was observed in 85% of cases even when mapping was repeated using different pacing sites. Ablation targeting DZs resulted in freedom from VT recurrence in approximately 70% of patients during a mean follow-up of 12 ± 10 months [ 13 ].

In our experience with functional substrate mapping, sites associated with VT termination frequently demonstrated a rotational activation pattern (RAP), pivoting around the edge of a conduction block during baseline sinus or ventricular-paced rhythm (Fig. 2 ). When the relationship between RAP and VT circuits was systematically evaluated, RAP was identified in approximately 70% of 33 VT morphologies in which VT termination by ablation or a perfect pace map with subsequent noninducibility was achieved [ 14 ]. A key feature of RAP is that it reflects not merely conduction delay but a rotational propagation pattern characterized by inward curvature of the wavefront pivoting around the edge of a conduction block. These electrophysiological characteristics suggest the presence of a localized line of conduction block forming the boundaries of the reentrant circuit. Among patients in which RAP was not apparent during mapping in sinus rhythm, additional mapping performed under ventricular pacing revealed newly emergent RAP in a subset of patients [ 27 ]. Mapping during pacing near the region of interest facilitates identification of the RAP and the line of conduction block, as delineation becomes difficult when activation wavefronts approaching from multiple directions converge and collide within the region (Fig. 3 ).

As a functional substrate mapping approach that captures dynamic electrophysiological properties, one strategy involves identifying sites exhibiting decrement-evoked potentials during ventricular extrastimulation [ 28 , 29 ]. Furthermore, dynamic substrate mapping during extrastimulation may allow more specific identification of arrhythmogenic substrate than conventional substrate mapping [ 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ].

When conduction abnormalities such as isochronal crowding, DZ, lines of conduction block (LOB), or RAP are identified during substrate mapping, it is essential to perform pace mapping to determine which sites represent critical conduction abnormalities related to the targeted VT. Because multiple regions exhibiting conduction abnormalities may coexist within the substrate, careful determination of the primary target associated with the targeted VT is of paramount importance (Fig. 4 ). During pace mapping, particular attention should be paid to sites where the QRS morphology abruptly changes from a poor to an excellent match [ 34 , 35 ], as well as to locations demonstrating multiple exit sites (MES), characterized by the emergence of more than one QRS morphology during pacing from the same site [ 36 ].

4. Three-Dimensional Arrhythmogenic Substrates VT circuits confined to a purely 2D plane are relatively uncommon. Simultaneous endocardial and epicardial mapping (SEEM), introduced by Tung and colleagues, represents a landmark investigation that directly demonstrated the 3D nature of VT circuits in humans [ 15 ]. Using SEEM, the majority of VT circuits involve nonuniform transmural conduction, rendering it difficult to fully delineate the reentrant pathway using surface-based mapping alone. A substantial proportion of VTs are sustained by entirely intramural (mid-myocardial) reentry, in which focal activation patterns are observed on both the endocardial and epicardial surfaces.

Building upon these observations, Nishimura and Tung proposed a conceptual framework in which VT circuits are understood as 3D hyperboloid structures rather than planar pathways [ 37 ]. In the hyperboloid model, the VT isthmus is defined as a 3D structure with hyperbolic geometry, and the reentrant circuit is constrained by fixed LOBs that form both lateral and depth boundaries. From this perspective, LOBs identified during sinus rhythm should not be interpreted merely as 2D barriers on a mapping surface, but rather as manifestations of depth-oriented boundaries within a 3D VT circuit. The presence of concealed LOBs that become apparent only with differential pacing maneuvers [ 37 ]. This concept is in line with the observation that RAP may be unmasked depending on the direction of the activation wavefront relative to the scar during mapping [ 27 ]. Therefore, substrate mapping findings such as LOBs, RAP, and DZs should be interpreted not as isolated surface phenomena, but as surface projections of a volumetric 3D circuit.

5. Ablation Strategies Based on Three-Dimensional Arrhythmogenic Substrates If VT circuits are understood as volumetric 3D structures rather than planar pathways, ablation strategies must be aligned with this conceptual framework. The concept of 3D VT circuits represents more than a theoretical advance; it carries important clinical implications that fundamentally reshape substrate-based ablation strategies. In particular, this framework provides a mechanistic explanation for why surface-limited ablation alone is often associated with suboptimal VT-free survival and why high-power or deep lesion formation may be required in selected cases. When the hyperboloid model of VT circuits is considered, identification of a LOB during sinus rhythm or paced rhythm suggests that ablation targeting regions adjacent to both sides of the LOB may be advantageous. We suggest that in patients in whom RAP around the LOB associated with a targeted VT is identified, localized ablation encompassing the RAP region may represent a rational ablation strategy [ 38 ]. Identification and intensive ablation of targeted RAP areas that were identified with high-density and high-resolution substrate mapping resulted in a high probability of freedom from VT recurrence, exceeding 80% in reported series [ 38 ].

When an intramural isthmus contributes to VT maintenance, conventional radiofrequency energy delivery from the endocardial or epicardial surface may be insufficient to create a transmural lesion. In such cases, it is crucial to identify segments of the critical isthmus that course closer to the mapped chamber surface, rather than targeting activation gaps located deep within the myocardial wall. These surface-adjacent components may represent more accessible and effective ablation targets within an otherwise intramural circuit.

To effectively interrupt conduction of the VT circuit, particular attention should be paid to the near-field components of bipolar electrograms. When using the QDOT Micro catheter (Biosense Webster) under the guidance of the CARTO3 system (Biosense Webster), the microelectrodes are designed to minimize far-field contamination and thus more accurately reflect true local activations. Consequently, the recorded signals predominantly represent activation of the immediately adjacent myocardial surface being mapped, and multiple-component or fractionated potentials are less frequently observed (Fig. 5 ). Using the EnSite mapping system (Abbott), regions exhibiting markedly high peak frequency along the VT circuit may reflect dominant near-field components recorded at the myocardial surface and may correspond to locally vulnerable areas. In contrast, segments of the circuit that are predominantly intramural may manifest as lower peak frequency values in recorded local ventricular potentials. Channels in which surviving superficial myocardium is strongly involved—and in which ablation lesions are more readily delivered—exhibit higher peak frequency values (Fig. 6 ), with thresholds above approximately 405 Hz associated with rapid VT termination during radiofrequency application [ 39 ]. Sites corresponding to the VT isthmus have been shown to exhibit both low bipolar voltage and elevated peak frequency during sinus rhythm or paced rhythm [ 40 ]. However, comparative analyses of electrograms from dominant VT circuits and bystander scar regions have demonstrated no significant difference in peak frequency between isthmus and nonparticipating scar tissue, indicating that peak frequency alone cannot reliably discriminate critical VT isthmuses from bystander substrates [ 41 ]. Accordingly, peak frequency should not be regarded as a standalone determinant of ablation targets but rather as an adjunctive parameter that must be integrated with circuit-dependent information, such as activation or entrainment mapping, or other functional substrate markers.

6. Approaches to Assess Intramural Arrhythmogenic Substrate Despite advances in high-resolution surface mapping, direct assessment of intramural conduction abnormalities remains one of the most significant unresolved challenges in VT ablation. When a component of a 3D VT circuit is located along the endocardial or epicardial surface, mapping may allow identification of a LOB corresponding to the depth boundary of the reentrant pathway. As discussed above, accurate delineation and ablation of LOB or regions of isochronal crowding during sinus rhythm can therefore be effective in interrupting VT circuits. In contrast, mid-myocardial reentry—characterized by absence of isthmus activation on both the endocardial and epicardial surfaces—often manifests as focal activation patterns on both surfaces. In such cases, LOB is frequently indistinct, rendering circuit interruption by conventional ablation strategies particularly challenging [ 38 ].

When substrate mapping fails to reveal clear wavefront discontinuity and a predominantly intramural mid-myocardial arrhythmogenic substrate is suspected, the following practical considerations may guide clinical decision-making.

6.1 Attention to Activation Gaps during VT Activation Mapping During VT activation mapping, sites demonstrating an activation gap within the VT cycle length—particularly around lines of conduction block, when identifiable—may suggest intramural conduction. This is especially relevant when the activation gap corresponds to the diastolic phase, indicating that the critical isthmus may be located intramurally. Based on these findings, the likely VT circuit can be conceptualized, and ablation targets can be selected accordingly.

6.2 Attention to Far-Field Potentials One approach to inferring the presence of intramural substrates involves careful assessment of far-field ventricular potentials. Ideally, accurate mapping requires precise delineation of local activation within scar tissue, which is best achieved by minimizing far-field effects and recording near-field ventricular electrograms using small electrodes with short interelectrode spacing [ 42 , 43 , 44 ]. However, several prior case reports have suggested that far-field ventricular signals may provide valuable information regarding VT activation occurring deeper than the mapped surface [ 45 , 46 ]. Such intramural activity may be preferentially accentuated in bipolar electrograms recorded with relatively wider interelectrode spacing. During VT mapping, adjustment of the window of interest to the diastolic phase, or annotation of the first deflection relative to the offset of the surface QRS complex, may allow capture of pre-systolic or diastolic far-field components originating from intramural activation (Fig. 7 ).

In contrast, when first-deflection annotation was applied, the activation sequence could be tracked from sites 1 through 7, and the map clearly demonstrated diastolic-phase activation propagating around the line of block (right panel). In substrate mapping, a similar concept can be applied. Although conventional 3D mapping strategies typically aim to minimize far-field effects in favor of near-field signal annotation, attention to abnormal far-field components—particularly delayed components or signals recorded in the temporal interval between split potentials—may provide complementary insights into intramural conduction abnormalities. Using the EnSite mapping system (Abbott), annotation of the offset of local ventricular electrograms can facilitate visualization of sites exhibiting intramural conduction abnormalities (Fig. 8 ). Isochronal crowding or LOB observed on surface maps should not necessarily be interpreted as representations of surface activation, but rather as projections of intramural conduction patterns onto the mapped chamber surface.

(B) When annotation was performed at the last deflection, including far-field components of the local electrograms, the deceleration zone became clearly apparent. 6.3 Mid-Myocardial Mapping Using a Microcatheter Direct mapping of intramural components of VT circuits has also been attempted using specialized techniques, such as insertion of guidewires or microelectrodes into small branches of the coronary venous system [ 47 , 48 ]. In particular, mapping of the interventricular septum using a microcatheter advanced into septal perforator branches via the distal coronary sinus may facilitate direct assessment of intramural activity. Furthermore, the interventricular septum can be mapped using over-the-wire catheters, such as the EPstar Fix AIV (2.7 Fr; Japan Lifeline, Tokyo, Japan), not only via coronary venous branches but also through selected branches of the coronary arterial system [ 49 ]. Nevertheless, real-time, comprehensive visualization of intramural conduction dynamics remains beyond the full capability of current clinical mapping systems.

6.4 Preprocedural Cardiac Imaging Preprocedural cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can be useful to evaluate the distribution of mid-myocardial scar and to support the identification of intramural substrate. Late gadolinium enhancement cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (LGE-MRI) represents the most robust modality for assessing the presence and spatial distribution of intramural scar, enabling preprocedural identification of 3D substrates that are not fully captured by surface-based mapping alone [ 50 , 51 , 52 ]. In particular, LGE-MRI provides unique insights into intramural scar architecture, which plays a central role in sustaining complex VT circuits. Preprocedural MDCT provides complementary anatomical and structural information, including wall thickness and scar distribution, and aids in identifying critical structures to support procedural planning and safety [ 53 , 54 ].
7. Rethinking Procedural Endpoints The concept of procedural endpoints in VT ablation warrants reconsideration in light of emerging insights into three-dimensional arrhythmogenic substrates.

Although VT noninducibility remains a widely used procedural endpoint, it has important limitations and is insufficient as a standalone marker of success. Within a three-dimensional framework, endpoints should focus on effective disruption of critical conduction abnormalities, supported by post-ablation remapping. However, in predominantly intramural substrates, where surface mapping is limited, VT termination and noninducibility may remain the only practical indicators of success. In this section, we discuss the conceptual framework of procedural endpoints in VT ablation.

7.1 The Role of VT Noninducibility Noninducibility of VT assessed by programmed electrical stimulation (PES) represents the procedural endpoint with a long history and substantial supporting evidence [ 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 ]. From a clinical standpoint, VT noninducibility offers a practical and readily assessable marker of acute procedural success and therefore continues to be widely adopted as a procedural endpoint. Nevertheless, reliance on VT inducibility assessed by PES is subject to several important limitations. VT induction is influenced by the effects of antiarrhythmic medications, alterations in autonomic tone related to sedation or general anesthesia, and variability in stimulation sites and pacing protocols. Moreover, repeated PES performed across multiple longitudinal evaluations may increase the likelihood of VT induction [ 59 ]. Conversely, substrate mapping—an indispensable component of current ablation strategies for scar-mediated VT—itself may modify VT inducibility through mechanical and electrophysiological effects on the myocardium [ 60 ].

In addition, because most patients with scar-related VT have concomitant heart failure and develop hemodynamic instability during VT, post-ablation PES carries a non-negligible risk of inducing nonclinical arrhythmias, particularly rapid monomorphic VT or polymorphic VT, which may adversely affect hemodynamic status. This concern is especially relevant in patients with high-risk profiles as defined by the PAINESD risk score (Pulmonary disease, Age, Ischemic cardiomyopathy, New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, Ejection fraction, Storm, Diabetes mellitus) [ 61 ] or the PAINES2D score, which incorporates scar volume as an additional parameter [ 62 ]. In such high-risk patients, aggressive pursuit of VT noninducibility through repeated PES should be avoided.

Furthermore, PES frequently induces nonclinical VTs that have not been observed in the patient’s spontaneous clinical course [ 63 ]. Whether all inducible VTs—including those with relatively short cycle lengths—should be targeted for ablation, or whether ablation should be confined to regions associated with the clinical VT, remains a matter of debate. This decision may need to be individualized, taking into account overall patient frailty, procedural duration, and intraprocedural hemodynamic tolerance. Accordingly, although VT noninducibility remains an important and valuable procedural endpoint, it is insufficient as a standalone determinant of procedural success. Particularly in the context of substrate-based ablation as the primary strategy, there is a clear need to reconsider and supplement procedural endpoints beyond VT noninducibility alone.

7.2 Rethinking Ablation Endpoints Based on Three-Dimensional Substrate Characterization Within a 3D conceptual framework, procedural success should no longer be defined solely by arrhythmia suppression, but by evidence of effective disruption of the critical conduction architecture sustaining the VT circuit.

Across multiple studies, complete elimination of abnormal or late potentials, as well as successful core isolation, has not been achievable in all patients; however, when such endpoints are attained, they are consistently associated with favorable VT-free survival [ 8 , 9 , 64 , 65 , 66 , 67 , 68 , 69 , 70 , 71 , 72 , 73 , 74 ]. Loss of myocardial capture during high-output pacing has been used as an indicator of sufficient lesion formation [ 10 , 65 , 75 ]. Although the optimal pacing output and pulse width required to define capture loss remain debated [ 76 ], the absence of capture with high-output pacing reasonably suggests local electrical unexcitability and provides supportive evidence of adequate lesion formation.

Clinical outcomes following intensive ablation of targeted regions encompassing DZ, wavefront discontinuity lines, and RAPs have demonstrated one-year freedom from VT recurrence rates of approximately 70–80% [ 13 , 38 , 77 ]. In patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy, VT-free survival rates approaching 80% have been reported using such targeted strategies, which are comparable to the 84% freedom from VT observed in ischemic cardiomyopathy patients undergoing extensive scar homogenization—despite the substantially longer ablation times required for homogenization [ 10 ].

These observations support the concept that effective modification of functionally defined conduction abnormalities—rather than indiscriminate scar elimination—may be sufficient to interrupt a volumetric reentrant circuit.

Accordingly, procedural endpoints should extend beyond VT noninducibility and incorporate accurate identification of abnormal conduction regions exhibiting wavefront discontinuity that are linked to the critical isthmus of the 3D VT circuit, followed by high-intensity ablation of these targeted sites. Ablation confined strictly to a single focal site is likely insufficient. Instead, ablation should encompass the critical site together with adjacent sites with wavefront discontinuities and local abnormal ventricular potentials within a defined surrounding area (Fig. 9 ). However, the extent to which the ablation area should be expanded beyond the immediately targeted region, including adjacent zones where abnormal electrograms are recorded, remains uncertain. If the critical isthmus represents only the surface expression of a deeper 3D pathway, limiting ablation to a visually apparent focal site may fail to achieve durable circuit disruption. Given that the critical isthmus of a 3D VT circuit may not always be directly represented on the mapped surface, delivering ablation over an adequately sized area surrounding the targeted site may increase the likelihood of intersecting a more superficially traversing component of the intramural isthmus. It should be acknowledged, however, that current data are insufficient to establish an optimal upper limit for the extent of the ablation area. Future prospective studies will be required to determine the minimal yet sufficient ablation area necessary to effectively suppress VT recurrence, although this may vary depending on the underlying cardiac pathology, intraprocedural hemodynamic stability, and VT inducibility. However, it appears prudent to avoid indiscriminate extension of ablation into normal-voltage myocardium lacking abnormal electrograms, even when the targeted site is situated within a scar border zone adjacent to preserved myocardium.

7.3 The Importance of Post-Ablation Remapping If the objective of ablation is disruption of a 3D reentrant substrate, post-ablation assessment should confirm modification of the underlying conduction architecture rather than merely the disappearance of isolated electrogram abnormalities.

Regardless of whether a broad modification strategy such as scar homogenization or core isolation is employed, or a more selective targeted ablation approach focusing on DZs or RAP is applied, post-ablation remapping plays a critical role in procedural assessment. In the context of targeted ablation, the key objective of remapping should not be limited to confirming the disappearance of abnormal electrograms. Rather, procedural endpoints should be evaluated from the perspective of whether the boundary conditions required to sustain a 3D reentrant circuit have been effectively disrupted.

Post-ablation remapping has been reported to demonstrate disappearance of RAP around the edge of LOB in approximately 70% of cases following ablation of targeted regions [ 38 ]. As RAP is generally localized adjacent to regions of latest activation, its disappearance may indicate interruption of downstream conduction pathways, in line with the concept of scar dechanneling. In addition, prior studies have demonstrated that endocardial ablation can, in selected cases, achieve transmural lesion formation, particularly in regions of reduced wall thickness, thereby eliminating epicardial substrate from the endocardial surface [ 78 ]. Furthermore, even in the absence of complete transmurality, endocardial ablation may disrupt interconnecting channels between endocardial and epicardial substrates, contributing to modification of intramural and subepicardial arrhythmogenic pathways.

These findings suggest that remapping can provide mechanistic confirmation of successful substrate modification. However, despite its intuitive appeal, robust evidence demonstrating that systematic post-ablation remapping with strategy modification based on remapping findings leads to improved long-term outcomes remains limited. Thus, post-ablation remapping should be viewed not simply as a confirmatory step, but as an integral component of a strategy aimed at validating 3D circuit interruption. Accordingly, further investigation is warranted to establish the prognostic value of remapping-guided procedural refinement.

7.4 Ablation of Intramural VT Circuits In substrate-based ablation, the goal extends beyond acute termination of VT. Emphasis should instead be placed on analyzing activation patterns and identifying critical conduction abnormalities linked to the targeted VT. In contrast, when substrate mapping fails to reveal clear wavefront discontinuity, determination of an appropriate ablation endpoint becomes substantially more challenging.

In the setting of predominantly intramural circuits, the disconnect between surface mapping findings and the true 3D isthmus becomes most apparent. Given the current lack of techniques that allow real-time and direct assessment of intramural conduction abnormalities, objective evaluation of ablation efficacy in such cases is limited. Under these circumstances, termination of VT during ablation and subsequent noninducibility may represent the only reliable indicators of procedural success (Fig. 10 ). Fig. 10.

Several alternative ablation strategies aimed at achieving greater lesion depth have been explored, including bipolar ablation, chemical ablation, high-power radiofrequency delivery using open-irrigated electrodes cooled with half-normal saline, and ultra–low-temperature cryoablation [ 79 , 80 , 81 , 82 , 83 , 84 ]. Among emerging energy modalities, pulsed field ablation (PFA) has attracted considerable interest owing to its myocardial selectivity and potential for deep lesion formation. By inducing irreversible electroporation, PFA creates lesions through a nonthermal mechanism, raising the possibility of modifying 3D arrhythmogenic substrates while minimizing collateral injury to adjacent structures such as coronary arteries, neural tissue, and the esophagus. Consistent with this rationale, accumulating evidence has begun to suggest the potential efficacy of PFA in the treatment of VT [ 85 , 86 , 87 , 88 , 89 ]. Future studies will be essential to clarify the role of PFA and other deep-penetrating ablation modalities in addressing intramural VT circuits and in redefining procedural endpoints for scar-related VT ablation.

However, irrespective of the technique or energy modality used, in the absence of established methods for direct intraprocedural assessment of intramural conduction abnormalities, VT termination during ablation and subsequent noninducibility may continue to serve as the most dependable indicators of procedural success. 8. Future Perspectives As the conceptual framework of scar-related VT shifts from a predominantly planar interpretation toward a volumetric 3D paradigm, future advances must aim not only at improving lesion delivery but also at enhancing visualization of the underlying conduction architecture.

Further refinement of our understanding of 3D arrhythmogenic substrates will require closer integration of preprocedural cardiac imaging with 3D electroanatomical mapping. Beyond purely structural assessment of scar, emerging imaging approaches have begun to incorporate functional perspectives, such as evaluation of regional activation slowing and conduction heterogeneity using advanced cardiac imaging techniques [ 90 , 91 , 92 ]. These functional imaging modalities may further enhance identification of arrhythmogenic substrates by bridging the gap between structural abnormalities and electrophysiological behavior.

Looking ahead, the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning with cardiac imaging and high-resolution 3D electroanatomical mapping holds substantial promise. Through computational modeling and simulation, these approaches may enable more sophisticated characterization of arrhythmia initiation and maintenance mechanisms, ultimately facilitating personalized ablation strategies tailored to patient-specific 3D substrates [ 93 , 94 , 95 , 96 , 97 , 98 ]. Ultimately, convergence of advanced imaging, mechanistically informed targeting, and precise energy delivery may redefine both the strategy and the procedural endpoints of scar-related VT ablation.

9. Limitations Targeted ablation strategies based on functional substrate mapping have several limitations. First, as noted above, this approach may be less applicable in cases of predominantly intramural (mid-myocardial) arrhythmogenic substrate, in which no obvious wavefront discontinuity related to the targeted VT can be identified within the mapped chamber. Second, functional substrate mapping requires high-density and high-resolution mapping; therefore, its accuracy is influenced not only by the mapping system and catheter but also, to a certain extent, by the skill and experience of the operator and mapper. Third, further investigation is needed to compare functional substrate–guided targeted ablation with conventional structural substrate–based ablation in terms of efficacy and safety, as well as to determine which patient populations may derive the greatest benefit from targeted approaches.

10. Conclusions This review highlights that, within a three-dimensional perspective of scar-related VT substrate, accurate identification of critical conduction abnormalities as ablation targets is essential. In this context, procedural assessment should be reconsidered to focus on effective disruption of these abnormalities, supported by post-ablation remapping, as a reflection of successful modification of the underlying three-dimensional substrate, rather than relying solely on conventional endpoints such as VT noninducibility. Intramural substrates remain a major challenge, underscoring the need for improved methods to assess intramural conduction and to achieve durable lesion formation.

Purpose of Review This review aims to evaluate the contemporary and evolving role of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging in arrhythmic risk stratification for patients with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, specifically focussing on dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy (NDLVC). This review synthesises current data on late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), parametric mapping, strain imaging and artificial intelligence (AI), and contextualises these among emerging genetic risk stratification approaches.

Recent Findings Left ventricular ejection fraction has been the cornerstone for guideline-based arrhythmic risk stratification in patients with DCM, despite limited precision. Observational data and meta-analyses have established the presence of replacement fibrosis through LGE-CMR as a powerful independent predictor of ventricular arrhythmias (VAs) and sudden cardiac death. Crucially, the absence of LGE identifies a low-risk cohort. Much recent focus has been on understanding whether more precise characterisation of scar can further enhance arrhythmic risk stratification, for example through scar quantification. Although data exists supporting a potential role for T1 mapping for arrhythmic risk prediction in this cohort, further research is required to support its widespread adoption. Emerging multimodal approaches using artificial intelligence and personalised computational “digital twins” are areas of important interest, offering scope for integration of imaging, electrocardiographic and genomic data layers.

Summary Arrhythmic risk stratification in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathies remains challenging despite significant advances. Progressive refinement in precision has accompanied a shift from a restrictive, functional assessment towards an integrated, substrate-driven precision model. CMR represents the cornerstone of this evolution.

Common to this highly heterogeneous group of patients is an underlying dynamic risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD), which most commonly occurs in this population due to ventricular arrhythmias (VAs). Estimating the risk of SCD, and implementing therapies to mitigate this, represents a critical component of the clinical management of these patients. These conditions are routinely classified based on their phenotype. Revised nomenclature from the 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies defines five distinct cardiomyopathy phenotypes. The focus of this review is the arrhythmic risk stratification of patients with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy (NDLVC), among whom there exists substantial clinical overlap.

DCM is among the most prevalent of NICMs, affecting approximately 1 in 250 individuals, and is defined as a heterogeneous primary myocardial disease characterised by left ventricular (LV) or biventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction, not explained solely by abnormal loading conditions or coronary artery disease [ 1 ]. NDLVC, a distinct clinical entity to DCM, is defined by the presence of non-ischaemic LV scarring or fatty replacement, with or without global LV hypokinesis, but in the absence of LV dilation [ 2 ]. Previous nomenclature utilised the term “hypokinetic non-dilated LV cardiomyopathy”, which described the cardiomyopathy subgroup with contractile impairment without cavity dilation [ 3 ]. The 2023 ESC Guidelines replaced this term with NDLVC, expanding the definition to encompass patients with or without systolic dysfunction, and formally recognising non-ischaemic myocardial scarring or fatty replacement as the critical element of this cardiomyopathy subgroup.

While epidemiological studies have shown a temporal linear decline in the rate of SCD in non-ischaemic DCM patients [ 4 ], the risk of arrhythmias and SCD in NICM remains significant. Among patients with NICM and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 35%, approximately 30% of deaths are arrhythmic in aetiology [ 5 ].

Extensive evidence exists to support the pathobiological mechanisms, notably scar-related macro-reentry, underlying VAs in DCM and NDLVC [ 6 ]. Pathological processes like fibro-fatty replacement and diffuse interstitial collagen deposition disrupt the uniform propagation of electrical conduction through the systemic uncoupling of adjacent cardiomyocytes [ 7 , 8 ]. These disruptions increase tissue resistance and create zones of slow conduction and functional block across the myocardium [ 9 ]. Within this fibrotic architecture, surviving myocyte bundles interspersed between dense scar form discrete arrhythmia channels – corridors of preserved but functionally abnormal conduction that serve as the electrophysiological substrate for stable reentrant circuits [ 10 , 11 ]. The structural heterogeneity imposed by progressive fibrosis creates the conditions necessary for both the initiation and perpetuation of VAs, including ventricular fibrillation (VF). Although there has been a correlation between scar burden and LVEF, it is feasible to have significant scar and arrhythmic substrate in patients with mildly reduced LVEF. Consequently, characterising this arrhythmogenic substrate is of paramount importance for accurate risk stratification.

For decades, the cornerstone of arrhythmic risk stratification and candidacy for primary prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) implantation has been centred on the LVEF, where a threshold of ≤ 35% has been universally adopted, alongside New York Heart Association (NYHA) class [ 12 ]. The foundational evidence supporting LVEF as the primary criteria for ICD candidacy stems from landmark trials such as DEFINITE and SCD-HeFT, alongside its adoption among the inclusion criteria in randomised controlled ICD trials (Table 1 ). While these trials demonstrated a mortality benefit for primary prevention ICDs in mixed or non-ischaemic cohorts, they were conducted in an era preceding the application of modern, highly effective heart failure pharmacotherapy.
