However, more recent clinical trials have brought into question the sensitivity of LVEF-based selection in identifying high-risk individuals. Notably, findings from major trials such as DANISH, which demonstrated ICD implantation did not improve survival in NICM patients with an LVEF ≤ 35%, have highlighted this [ 16 ]. This has been further supported by more recent studies, including a large 2024 observational study where two key findings were made: (1) an LVEF < 35% failed to reach significance as a predictor of SCD or VAs when myocardial fibrosis was included as a co-variable, suggesting LVEF may merely act as a surrogate for underlying myocardial scarring, and (2) the absence of myocardial fibrosis on visual assessment virtually excluded the risk of SCD and ventricular arrhythmias in the long term, regardless of the patient’s LVEF (negative predictive value: 98%) [ 19 ].

The legacy of the DANISH trial and subsequent studies lies in the fact that LVEF is a profoundly imprecise tool for arrhythmic risk stratification, where LVEF has never been shown to be a reliable predictor of VAs in NICM [ 20 ]. While a low LVEF is a robust marker of advanced myocardial disease and global mortality risk, it does not effectively discriminate patients whose main threat is an arrhythmic event from those who are more likely to succumb to pump failure. Indeed, most SCD events in the general population occur in individuals with an LVEF > 35% (who would not have fulfilled ICD implantation criteria), while conversely, many patients with severely depressed LVEF never experience malignant arrhythmias [ 21 – 23 ]. Collectively, this highlights an urgent need for more precise stratification tools (Fig. 1 ).

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) has emerged as the gold standard non-invasive modality for comprehensive myocardial tissue characterisation [ 24 , 25 ]. Through methods such as late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), parametric mapping and advanced functional deformation tracking, CMR provides a high-fidelity spatial and temporal representation of the myocardium. Recent ESC and ACC/AHA guidelines have also explicitly recognised the importance of CMR-derived metrics in refining risk stratification algorithms for NICM [ 26 ]. This review synthesises the contemporary evidence surrounding CMR modalities in evaluating arrhythmic risk in DCM and NDLVC, exploring the clinical utility of CMR parameters, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and positions these alongside the emerging role of clinical genetics.

Cardiovascular MRI Parameters and Clinical Utility Late Gadolinium Enhancement Gadolinium-based contrast agents are extracellular paramagnetic agents which distribute freely into extracellular space but are unable to cross intact myocyte cell membranes. In areas of prior myocardial necrosis, the cellular architecture is replaced by dense, biochemically inert collagen networks, resulting in an expanded extracellular space and thus, delayed contrast washout [ 27 ]. Electrophysiologically, replacement fibrosis serves as the requisite anatomical substrate for abnormal electrical conduction and arrhythmias [ 7 , 28 ]. These regions of replacement fibrosis appear hyperintense on specialised T1-weighted inversion recovery sequences, against the dark background of healthy myocardium [ 29 ].

The prognostic utility of LGE in NICM is supported by a large volume of observational data. Gulati et al. initially demonstrated a powerful association between the presence of mid-wall LGE and SCD in NICM, with this remaining an independent predictor after adjustment for LVEF and conventional clinical variables [ 30 ]. This has been further replicated and validated in other cohorts. Most recently, an exhaustive systematic review and meta-analysis by Eichhorn et al. aggregated data from 103 studies encompassing nearly 30,000 patients with DCM. The meta-analyses established the binary presence of LGE – seen in approximately 40% of patients with NICM – was a strong predictor of adverse outcomes, displaying its strongest association with VAs and SCD (HR 2.69) among all endpoints evaluated [ 5 , 31 ]. Other meta-analyses have corroborated this, where the mere presence of LGE in DCM increases mortality three-fold and the risk of SCD or aborted SCD four-fold, compared to matched patients without LGE [ 32 , 33 ] (Fig. 1 ).

Beyond visual presence, there has been much interest in whether a deeper phenotypic characterisation of scar provides superior risk stratification. One such characteristic is the fibrosis mass/extent, where a number of studies have demonstrated that higher scar mass/extent is associated with greater arrhythmic risk [ 19 , 34 ]. A limitation to this approach relates to a lack of uniformity in scar quantification methods and intrinsic differences that may emerge between scar quantification undertaken on patients scanned using different magnetic field strengths, using different contrast agents or between those analysed across different software platforms. One study demonstrated that a small amount of LGE (e.g. 0% to 0.71% of LV mass) was associated with a substantial increase in risk compared to patients without LGE, suggesting a non-linear dose-response relationship [ 21 , 35 , 36 ]. A more recent study proposed a dichotomised cutoff, identifying an LGE burden of ≥ 7.5% as the strongest predictor of VAs [ 37 ]. A larger 2-centre study of 1,714 patients with NICM quantified total fibrosis mass, where it was found patients with > 10 g of total fibrosis had a nine-fold increased hazard for a composite endpoint of SCD, aborted SCD or VF (HR 9.17; 95% CI 4.64-18.1) compared to patients with no fibrosis [ 19 ].

In addition to overall burden, fibrosis position may play an important role in risk stratification. In DCM, septal involvement is most commonly observed, where LGE predominantly manifests in a mid-wall distribution [ 36 , 38 , 39 ]. Indeed, mid-wall LGE, particularly localised to the basal septal and lateral walls, has been shown to strongly increase the risk of life-threatening VAs and SCD risk and mortality [ 30 , 35 , 40 ]. This has been reflected in a large contemporary European dataset: DERIVATE registry’s updated Risk Score 2.0, affirming that the presence and location of mid-wall scar confer additive, independent risk [ 41 ].

Beyond mass and position, the scar pattern might hold additional prognostic significance. Advanced imaging analyses have identified a particularly malignant topological variant known as the “ring-like” LGE pattern, observed in both DCM and NDLVC patients [ 39 ]. This is characterised by a contiguous, circumferential mid-wall or subepicardial scarring spanning multiple myocardial segments [ 42 , 43 ]. This pattern has been associated with a high burden of VAs and increased risk of malignant arrhythmias, but importantly, not an impairment in LVEF, further highlighting the limitations of LVEF as a proxy for ICD implantation [ 39 ].

Nevertheless, there remains a lack of research into the diagnostic and prognostic value of LGE in patients who fall outside the traditional bounds of severe systolic dysfunction. This includes patients with “mild” DCM (characterised by an LVEF > 40%) and those with “recovered/improved” DCM (also termed HFimpEF: heart failure with improved ejection fraction), whose LVEF has improved following treatment with guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) [ 44 ]. Notably, Halliday et al. demonstrated that the presence of LGE is strongly associated with an increased risk of SCD in DCM patients with mild and moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction [ 35 ]. Crucially, LVEF is an inherently dynamic parameter that often changes over time in these conditions. As a result of this, a single snapshot of functional remodelling cannot be equated with a reduced risk of SCD [ 45 – 47 ].

Parametric Mapping While the clinical and prognostic validity of LGE for mapping replacement fibrosis is firmly established, this correlates histologically with replacement fibrosis and does not capture interstitial fibrosis. While replacement scar signifies dense, irreversible collagen deposition, interstitial fibrosis represents an earlier, globally distributed remodelling phase that remains potentially reversible. CMR parametric mapping, specifically T1 mapping and the derivation of the extracellular volume (ECV) fraction, permits quantitative assessment of myocardial interstitial fibrosis. Native T1 mapping evaluates the relaxation time of myocardial tissue; prolonged native T1 relaxation times, often coupled with shortened post-contrast T1 times, are indicative of expanded interstitial volume, serving as a surrogate for fibrotic remodelling [ 48 ]. By integrating both pre- and post-contrast measurements, clinicians can derive the ECV fraction, which acts as a sensitive proxy for the percentage of the interstitial space expanded by fibrosis.

The prognostic relevance of CMR parametric mapping in NICM was evaluated by Puntmann et al. in a multicentre study of 637 patients. This demonstrated that native T1 and ECV fraction were associated with mortality and heart failure outcomes. In multivariable analysis, native T1 emerged as the sole independent predictor of the study’s endpoints [ 49 ]. It is important to recognise, however, that these endpoints were defined as all-cause mortality and a heart failure composite, rather than arrhythmic events. Subsequent research has bridged this gap by studying parametric mapping parameters in relation to VAs. Chen et al. demonstrated that native T1 is an independent predictor of appropriate ICD therapy or documented sustained VAs in patients with NICM, where patients faced a 1.4-fold increased risk of the primary arrhythmic endpoint for every 10 ms increment in non-contrast native T1 [ 50 ].

This was further corroborated by Li et al. in a large cohort of 659 patients with DCM, which found native T1 and ECV possess significant prognostic value, and importantly, established a combined assessment of LGE, T1 and ECV provides optimal risk stratification [ 51 ]. This study also noted that parametric mapping provides orthogonal risk discrimination for patients who do not exhibit regional scarring on LGE. In LGE negative patients, mean native T1 and mean ECV fraction were the only independent variables associated with cardiovascular death. It is important to note that this study was not focused on arrhythmic endpoints, and so it remains unknown whether ECV may have utility in arrhythmic risk stratification of LGE negative NICM patients. Studies specifically probing this would be challenging to conduct due to the low incidence of VAs in this subgroup.

In a further study, Di Marco et al. found that an ECV threshold of ≥ 30% was significantly associated with an elevated risk of VAs in patients with NICM, demonstrating a 14.1-fold increased risk even after adjustment for the presence of LGE and an LVEF ≤ 35% [ 52 ]. Their analysis of 618 patients with NICM showed incorporating this ECV threshold into risk models reclassified approximately 32% of the study population compared to using LVEF alone. Notably, this approach identified that 71% of patients who would traditionally have been classified as high-risk based on an LVEF ≤ 35% were actually at low risk for arrhythmic events. A simple clinical model integrating LGE, LVEF ≤ 35%, and ECV ≥ 30% achieved a high predictive performance (Harrell’s C-statistic: 0.820 to 0.885). Interestingly, native T1 mapping and global longitudinal strain (GLS) in this specific cohort did not provide additional independent prognostic value for the arrhythmic endpoint [ 52 ].

A 2025 meta-analysis by Marchini et al. evaluating T1 mapping and ECV in non-ischaemic DCM patients demonstrated both parameters are independently associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and arrhythmic outcomes [ 53 ]. Each 1% absolute increase in ECV was associated with a 37% increase in the risk for MACE (HR 1.37; 95% CI 1.29–1.44), while each 10 ms elevation in native T1 time was associated with a 7% increase in the risk of MACE (HR 1.07; 95% CI 1.04–1.09). Native T1 mapping also demonstrated significant prognostic value for arrhythmic-related events specifically, with a pooled HR of 1.09 (95% CI 1.07–1.12) per 10 ms increase.

An important caveat in interpreting native T1 data is its limited external generalisability. Native T1 values are strongly dependent on magnetic field strength, being substantially longer at 3T than at 1.5T, and are further influenced by the mapping sequence (e.g. MOLLI, ShMOLLI or SASHA), vendor and acquisition parameters [ 54 ]. Consequently, normal reference ranges must be established for each scanner and sequence and validated in healthy controls at each centre. Absolute native T1 thresholds derived in one cohort therefore cannot readily be transferred to another, and a single universally applicable cutoff is unlikely to be achievable. By contrast, ECV is derived from the ratio of pre- and post-contrast changes in myocardial and blood-pool T1, corrected for haematocrit, which partially normalises for field strength and sequence-related differences [ 54 ]. This makes ECV less subject to variation in magnetic field strength and parametric mapping sequence (Fig. 1 ).

Despite the evidence surrounding T1 and ECV, there is currently a paucity in the literature evaluating T2 mapping of arrhythmic risk stratification in DCM and NDLVC. While T2-weighted imaging is essential for identifying myocardial oedema in acute inflammatory states like myocarditis, its role in characterising the chronic pro-arrhythmic substrate of DCM remains unclear.

Left Ventricular Strain Imaging Myocardial deformation analysis, widely known as strain imaging, evaluates myocardial shortening, thickening and lengthening throughout the cardiac cycle. Feature-tracking cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR-FT) has emerged as a highly reproducible method for this, by utilising standard steady-state free precession (SSFP) cine images to mathematically track tissue voxel displacement over time, thereby calculating the precise regional deformation of myocardial fibres by quantifying myocardial shortening, thickening and lengthening [ 55 , 56 ].

Global longitudinal strain (GLS) evaluates the shortening of subendocardial, longitudinally-oriented myocardial fibres [ 57 ]. These fibres are particularly susceptible to early microvascular ischaemia, elevated wall stress and initial fibrotic infiltration. In one large multicentre study involving 1,012 patients with DCM by Romano et al., impaired CMR-derived LV GLS was proven to be a powerful, independent predictor of mortality, incremental to LVEF and LGE. After adjustment for clinical parameters, LVEF and the extent of LGE, every 1% absolute reduction in GLS conferred a nearly 89% increased relative risk of all-cause mortality (HR 1.89 per %; p < 0.001) [ 58 ]. However, it is important to note that no data on arrhythmic events were reported in this study. A further study involving 355 DCM patients with mildly reduced EF (LVEF ≥ 40%) found LV GLS was not associated with SCD, and LGE presence was the only predictor of SCD [ 59 ]. Currently there is a lack of data to suggest that LV GLS may be a useful imaging parameter in arrhythmic risk stratification in NICM. This follows mechanistically, as LV GLS is ultimately a metric of contractile performance, and hence is not a direct measure of arrhythmic substrate.

Artificial Intelligence While conventional CMR analysis has substantially advanced the field, it remains constrained by factors such as inter-observer variability, time-intensive post-processing demands and the inherent biological limitation of human visual assessment of LGE. The burgeoning fields of AI, deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML) are shifting CMR to an automated, high-throughput and high-dimensional investigation.

One such advance made in arrhythmic risk stratification is the transition from human-derived algorithms to deep multimodal learning architectures. SCD is inherently a multifactorial event, influenced by complex interactions between genetics, structural pathology, electrical conduction, systemic comorbidities, and patient circumstance. Recognising this complexity, Lai et al. have recently developed a Multimodal AI for Ventricular Arrhythmia Risk Stratification (MAARS) model. It is important to note that while MAARS has only been developed and validated on hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) patients, this serves as a proof-of-concept for the development of similar models in DCM and NDLVC patients. MAARS is an AI framework utilising an advanced transformer-based neural network in order to integrate contrast-enhanced CMR images with electronic health records, clinical reports and continuous ECG parameters. This approach allows for the discovery of previously hidden, highly complex architectural fibrosis patterns that precipitate arrhythmias, where the model is capable of identifying subtle, high-risk ECG features. Indeed, MAARS has demonstrated strong predictive accuracy for SCD due to arrhythmias, yielding area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values approaching 0.89 and vastly outperforming existing 2024 ACC/AHA and 2022 ESC guidelines [ 60 ].

Another growing application is the development of the “digital twin”, a highly personalised, in silico mathematical model of a patient’s heart [ 61 , 62 ]. These dynamic virtual patient representations integrate multi-modal data to simulate clinical scenarios and treatment strategies, allowing for the forecasting of clinical outcomes. One such application was demonstrated by O’Hara et al., who developed personalised virtual-heart replicas to assess SCD. By fusing data from two different CMR modalities – LGE to identify focal scar and T1 mapping to visualise diffuse fibrosis – high-fidelity digital models of the patient-specific arrhythmogenic substrate were created. These digital twins achieved 80.1% accuracy in forecasting future VA events, significantly outperforming conventional clinical risk predictors from existing guidelines such as the ESC [ 63 ].

Beyond these static mechanistic models, the future of arrhythmic risk stratification lies in the transition to “active” digital twins that maintain a continuous cyber-physical connection with the patient. This next generation of technology will integrate real-time data from wearables such as smartwatches, alongside historical data like genomics and medical records. The integration of these multimodal data streams into deep learning architectures and generative AI models may allow the synthesis of missing cardiac data and the simulation of 3D scarring patterns [ 64 ]. By doing so, clinicians can move towards a dynamic, individualised risk profile that evolves in real-time as a patient’s condition changes or new therapies are introduced.

Role of Genetics Given that it is now recognised that between 20% and 30% of DCM cases are familial in origin, of which 40% have an identifiable monogenic cause, identifying genetically-predisposed individuals at a higher risk of malignant VAs is paramount for arrhythmic risk stratification [ 65 ]. Extensive research has isolated a specific subset of genes associated with a malignant clinical trajectory. These high-risk loci encompass variants affecting the nuclear envelope (e.g. LMNA , TMEM43 ), cytoskeletal and Z-disk proteins (e.g. FLNC ), desmosomal complexes (e.g. DSP , DSG2 , DSC2 , PKP2 ), RNA-splicing elements (e.g. RBM20 ) and calcium-handling proteins (e.g. PLN ) [ 2 , 66 – 70 ] (Fig. 1 ). The impact of these variants was elucidated by Escobar-Lopez et al., whose study analysed an extensively characterised cohort of 1,203 genotyped patients with non-ischaemic DCM. Important prognostic signals were observed in this study, where malignant VAs occurred in nearly 30% of patients harbouring high-risk arrhythmic genotypes. In multivariate regression models adjusted for LVEF and NYHA class, both the genotype and LGE were strong independent predictors of malignant VAs [ 71 ].

A study by Stroeks et al. utilising unsupervised machine learning on a multicentre cohort of 534 genotype-positive DCM patients further highlights the importance of considering the genetic architecture in arrhythmic risk stratification. By contrasting a “phenotype-first” clustering approach (grouping patients by clinical and imaging similarities) against a “genotype-first” approach, the analysis revealed phenotypic clusters correlated poorly with the underlying genotype [ 72 ]. More importantly, the genotype-first approach was vastly superior in predicting clinical outcomes, including malignant VAs. These findings collectively highlight that genetic architecture and CMR-derived tissue characterisation are not independent risk domains but complementary layers of the same arrhythmic risk spectrum: the genotype defines susceptibility, while LGE defines the structural platform through which this susceptibility can produce arrhythmia.

Limitations Despite multiple studies highlighting the capabilities of CMR in arrhythmic risk stratification, its widespread implementation faces several limitations. CMR is highly resource-intensive, requiring costly infrastructure, specialised scanning protocols and clinicians trained in reading and interpreting imaging. Indeed, access is often restricted to tertiary academic centres, creating geographical disparities [ 73 ]. Additionally, the extensive data linking CMR-defined fibrosis to SCD is predominantly derived from retrospective and prospective observational cohorts. There remains a critical absence of large-scale RCT data showing ICD implantation based primarily on CMR parameters such as the presence of LGE definitively improves overall survival compared to current standard of care.

A major technical hurdle is the lack of consensus regarding the standardisation of fibrosis quantification methodologies. Many methodologies exist for quantifying fibrosis, and while a relative scar burden or total mass cutoff provides compelling prognostic arrhythmic risk stratification in individual studies, there is no universally accepted methodology. These include manual visual scoring methods and various semi-automated signal thresholding techniques such as the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) method and the n -standard deviation (e.g. 2-SD, 5-SD) approaches calculated above normal remote myocardium. This lack of technical standardisation introduces substantial inter-observer, software and inter-vendor variability, making it clinically challenging to uniformly apply absolute quantitative cutoffs across different institutions.

Future Directions The evolving landscape of risk stratification in NICM is shifting away from a singular reliance on LVEF and global functional metrics, and towards a more refined approach. This evolution focuses on the direct visualisation of the pro-arrhythmic substrate, tissue-level characterisation on CMR and the integration of multi-dimensional data to better identify patients who will derive a true benefit from ICD therapy.

Emerging CMR Modalities Emerging CMR techniques may offer the potential to further refine this substrate-driven approach by looking beyond macroscopic scarring. Advanced microstructural imaging such as diffusion-tensor cardiovascular magnetic resonance (DT-CMR) maps the three-dimensional spatial alignment of myocardial fibres and sheetlets, allowing for cardiac microstructure to be studied at the level of the cardiomyocyte. While existing studies have demonstrated significant microstructural abnormalities in DCM patients, the specific utility of DT-CMR to predict SCD has not yet been formally assessed. Some existing work in HCM has shown early promise for DT-CMR as an emerging imaging biomarker of arrhythmic risk [ 74 ].

Ongoing Clinical Validation Central to these efforts are several clinical trials designed to move the field towards a more personalised, substrate-driven model of care. The ongoing BRITISH trial (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05568069 ) is a multicentre, UK-based randomised controlled trial (RCT). This study will enrol 1,252 patients with NICM and LVEF ≤ 35% with LGE on routine CMR. Eligible patients will be randomised to either an interventional arm receiving an ICD or a control arm receiving an implantable loop recorder (ILR) or cardiac resynchronisation therapy pacemaker (CRT-P). The primary endpoint is the comparison of all-cause mortality [ 75 ]. Parallel efforts are also being made, where the CMR-GUIDE HF trial (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03993730 ) is extending this investigational paradigm to patients with mild-to-moderate systolic dysfunction (LVEF 36-50%) with LGE detected on CMR [ 76 ].

Conclusions The paradigm for arrhythmic risk stratification in NICM is undergoing a fundamental transition from functional assessment to substrate-based precision medicine. CMR is now established as an effective modality in delivering this. Importantly, the convergence of genotype-specific data with CMR imaging holds significant promise by combining structural remodelling and genetic susceptibility as synergistic layers of risk. While the results of landmark trials like BRITISH and CMR-GUIDE HF are still awaited, the current body of evidence suggests that an integrated, multiparametric approach, centred around CMR, is the future of personalised SCD prevention in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathies.

Background/Objectives: Sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a potentially life-threatening arrhythmia requiring prompt Emergency Department (ED) assessment and management. However, data on its frequency, real-world treatment, and prognosis in the ED remain limited. We aimed to describe the clinical characteristics, acute management, and short- and long-term outcomes of patients presenting with VT. Methods: We retrospectively included consecutive patients presenting to the ED between January 2018 and December 2024 with a primary diagnosis of sustained VT with a pulse. We collected baseline characteristics, hemodynamic status, underlying cardiac disease, and acute treatment. In-hospital events and 30-day and 1-year outcomes were assessed. Results: A total of 103 patients were identified, accounting for approximately 0.025% of all ED visits during the study period; 84.5% were male. Chest pain (31.1%) and palpitations (25.2%) were the most common presenting symptoms. Structural heart disease was present in 90% of the cases, predominantly of ischemic origin (61%). Nearly half of the patients (49.5%) had a prior history of VT. Electrical cardioversion was performed in 28.2% of the cases. The majority of the patients (95/103; 92%) required hospitalization. Mortality was 4.9% at 30 days and 17% at 1 year. After adjustment for age, a left ventricular ejection fraction ≤ 30% and in-hospital arrhythmic recurrence were independently associated with 1-year mortality. Conclusions: Sustained VT is an uncommon but high-risk ED presentation, mainly affecting patients with ischemic structural heart disease. A discrepancy was observed between real-world clinical practice and guideline recommendations. Introduction Ventricular tachycardia (VT) represents the most common cause of wide-complex tachycardia. Sustained ventricular tachycardia is defined as a ventricular arrhythmia lasting more than 30 s or leading to hemodynamic compromise within 30 s and requiring intervention. These arrhythmias can arise from, or involve, specialized conducting tissue as well as ventricular myocardium. VT can occur in structurally normal or abnormal hearts and can be hemodynamically tolerated or not. Ischemic heart disease is the most common cause of ventricular tachycardia, and VT has a wide range of clinical presentations, including palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, syncope, and cardiac arrest [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]. The 2022 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Guidelines emphasize a structured approach to ventricular arrhythmias, integrating prompt treatment of the acute episode with identification of the underlying substrate and individualized risk stratification for sudden cardiac death. In patients with sustained VT, immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion is recommended in the presence of hemodynamic instability, while electrical cardioversion or intravenous antiarrhythmic therapy may be considered in hemodynamically tolerated monomorphic VT, according to the clinical context and the safety of procedural sedation. Management should also include the identification and correction of reversible triggers, as well as early consideration of catheter ablation and implantable cardioverter–defibrillator therapy in selected high-risk patients [ 4 ]. Furthermore, accumulating evidence suggests that stellate ganglion block may represent a valuable adjunctive or bridging intervention in patients with refractory ventricular arrhythmias and electrical storm [ 5 , 6 ]. Nevertheless, in real-world settings, the immediate availability of invasive procedures and of the personnel, expertise, and resources required to safely deliver procedural sedation and analgesia may affect treatment selection and adherence to guideline-recommended care.

However, information on clinical characteristics, acute management and outcomes of patients with sustained VT in an emergency department (ED) is still limited. The aim of the present study was to provide a detailed description of clinical characteristics, presentation, treatment and prognosis of patients who were admitted to the emergency department of a tertiary care hospital for sustained VT.

2. Methods 2.1. Study Design and Population This is a single-center retrospective study including consecutive patients with sustained VT presenting to the ED of the Fondazione IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo of Pavia, which handles approximately 5000 patients per month. We reviewed the medical records of patients who presented with sustained VT (ICD-9-CM diagnostic code 427.1, ‘Paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia’) and were treated in this ED between January 2018 and December 2024. All potentially eligible cases identified through ICD-9-CM code 427.1 underwent manual review of the electronic medical record, including available 12-lead ECG recordings, clinical documentation, and ICD interrogation reports. Only patients with confirmed sustained VT with a pulse were included in the final analysis. Patients with wide QRS supraventricular tachycardia, non-sustained VT and those with pulseless VT were excluded.

2.2. Clinical Management and Follow-Up All patients had their medical history recorded and underwent physical examination, 12-lead ECG recording, routine laboratory testing, and chest X-ray. For those patients presenting with ongoing VT, the diagnosis was based on clinical history and current standard 12-lead ECG criteria [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ], including: absence of an RS complex in all precordial leads; an R–S interval > 100 ms in any precordial lead; presence of atrioventricular dissociation; fusion or capture beats; extreme axis deviation (from −90° to +180°); and morphological criteria for VT in the precordial leads. In patients presenting to the ED with an implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), the diagnosis of appropriate VT therapy was confirmed by ICD interrogation and retrieval of the clinical episode. Patients were considered stable if they had stable vital signs, including systolic blood pressure > 90 mmHg and absence of signs of end-organ hypoperfusion.

Information on ED management was collected by reviewing patients’ ED records. Data on whether patients were discharged or admitted to the hospital, and to which unit (Cardiology ward, Intensive Care Unit, General Intensive Care, or other), were also collected. Clinical outcomes and treatments received until hospital discharge were retrieved from patients’ medical records. Moreover, follow-up information at 30 days and 1 year was obtained by reviewing re-access and death registries or through telephone contact with patients or caregivers to assess clinical status.

2.3. Endpoint Definitions Beyond describing clinical management during the ED stay, our objective was to portray patient outcomes during the subsequent hospitalization. To achieve this aim, we defined two in-hospital endpoints to evaluate the prognosis of our cohort: (1) a clinical endpoint , defined as a composite of in-hospital mortality, need for vasoactive drugs, and/or intra-aortic balloon pump; and (2) an arrhythmic endpoint , defined as the need for antiarrhythmic drugs, ICD interventions, stellate ganglion block, electrical cardioversion, or external defibrillation for relapsing ventricular arrhythmias occurring after the index episode and beyond the ED stay.

2.4. Statistical Analysis Categorical variables were expressed as absolute numbers and percentages. Continuous variables were reported as median, minimum, and maximum values. Normality of distribution for continuous variables was initially assessed using histograms and the Shapiro–Wilk test. In cases of normally distributed data, Bartlett’s test was applied to assess homogeneity of variances. When both normal distribution and homogeneity of variances were confirmed, a t -test was then performed. Conversely, in the presence of abnormal distribution and/or heterogeneity of variances, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used. For categorical variables, either the Chi-square test or Fisher’s test was applied, depending on sample size.

Results were considered statistically significant at a p -value < 0.05. For parameters reaching statistical significance, a logistic regression model was performed, and p -values and odds ratios (OR) were reported. A preliminary bivariate analysis was conducted on key variables, adjusting for age, in order to identify potential 1-year mortality associations. Based on these findings, a multivariate logistic regression model was built. Missing data were imputed using the median for continuous variables and the mode for categorical variables. Missing data accounted for less than 5% of observations across all variables included in the database and for less than 3% of observations for the variables entered into the regression model. Survival analysis was performed using Kaplan–Meier curves for the overall population and stratified by the recurrence of arrhythmic events. For patients who were lost to follow-up, the date of last medical contact was considered. Statistical analysis was performed using R version 4.4.2.

3. Results 3.1. Clinical Endpoints During the study period, nearly 400,000 patients were admitted to the ED. Of these, 103 showed sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT), accounting for approximately 0.025% of all visits. The final study population included 103 patients, of whom 87 were male (84.4%) and 16 were female (15.5%). The median age at ED admission was 71 years (range 24–96), and the median body mass index (BMI) was 26 kg/m 2 .

Table 1 summarizes the relevant medical history and clinical characteristics of the enrolled patients. As shown in Figure 1 , 90% of patients had a previously diagnosed structural heart disease, predominantly of ischemic etiology (61%). Specifically, six patients presented with acute or subacute myocardial infarction, while 50 had a history of chronic ischemic heart disease without acute events. Dilated non-ischemic cardiomyopathy was observed in 15.2% of patients, valvular heart disease in 9.8%, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in 7.6%, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in 2.2%. Additionally, one patient had a dilated hypokinetic cardiomyopathy with arrhythmogenic features not yet fully characterized; one had dilated hypokinetic cardiomyopathy associated with Emery–Dreifuss syndrome; one had dilated cardiomyopathy with non-compaction features; and one had cardiac sarcoidosis.

Among patients with an available standard 12-lead ECG documenting the index arrhythmic episode, monomorphic VT was substantially more common than polymorphic VT. The most recent pre-admission assessment of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) indicated marked impairment of left ventricular systolic function, with a median LVEF of 35%. Only 15% of patients had a previously documented LVEF ≥ 50%. Regarding arrhythmic history, the index ED presentation represented a recurrence of VT in 49.5% of patients. Previous catheter ablation for VT had been performed in 18.1% of patients, whereas cardiac sympathetic denervation had been performed in 2.0%. Moreover, 63.7% of the patients had an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). Among ICD carriers, 44.6% had a single-chamber device, 10.8% a dual-chamber device, 41.5% a cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator (CRT-D), and 3.1% a subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD). Chronic antiarrhythmic therapy was prescribed in 85 patients; treatment regimens are summarized in Figure 2 .

3.2. Acute Management in the ED Among the 65 patients presenting with ongoing sustained VT, 44 were hemodynamically stable and 21 were hemodynamically unstable. First-line treatment according to hemodynamic status is shown in Figure 3 . Pharmacological therapy, predominantly amiodarone, was the most frequently selected initial strategy in hemodynamically stable patients, whereas electrical cardioversion (ECV) was used most often in hemodynamically unstable patients.

In the subgroup of hemodynamically stable patients, 25 were first treated with amiodarone, six with lidocaine, 10 underwent electrical cardioversion (ECV), and three were managed with manual overdrive pacing and/or ICD reprogramming. Among hemodynamically unstable patients, ECV was the most frequently used first-line treatment, performed in 10 patients (less than 50%). Six patients initially received amiodarone, and three received lidocaine. One patient underwent percutaneous stellate ganglion block (SGB) as the initial intervention, and one was treated with manual overdrive pacing and/or ICD reprogramming.

In the overall cohort, all treatments administered in the ED were recorded, including sequential therapies required to achieve arrhythmia termination. Treatment details are summarized in Table 2 . Amiodarone (50.5%) and lidocaine (19.4%) were the most frequently used antiarrhythmic agents. No patient received procainamide or verapamil in the ED. Procainamide was administered only after hospital admission in four patients managed in the coronary intensive care unit. Electrical cardioversion was performed in 20 subjects; specifically, in 69% of these cases, it was chosen as first-line therapy. Finally, eight patients underwent percutaneous stellate ganglion blockade during the hospital stay. Among patients with an ICD, 68.7% had documented automatic or manual ICD interventions.

3.3. Clinical Course During Hospitalization Ninety-two percent of the patients were hospitalized, mainly in the coronary intensive care unit ( Figure 4 ). The median length of stay was 10 days, with a minimum of 3 days and a maximum of 81 days. During hospitalization, 25.8% of patients underwent electrophysiological study, and approximately 75% of them received ablation of the arrhythmic substrate. Nine patients received an ICD: three were implanted with a single-chamber ICD, three with a subcutaneous ICD, two with a dual-chamber ICD, and one patient received a CRT-D. Four patients underwent cardiac denervation, while coronary angiography was performed in 32.3% of the patients, of whom 33% required percutaneous coronary intervention.

During the hospital stay, 27 patients (26,2%) experienced one of the clinical endpoints as previously defined. Specifically, two patients died during hospitalization, 11 patients needed vasoactive drugs and/or an intra-aortic balloon pump. Furthermore, 36 patients (34.9%) experienced at least one of the arrhythmic endpoints as previously described. More specifically, 51 patients required additional intravenous antiarrhythmic therapy, 14 experienced ICD interventions, four underwent stellate ganglion block, and eight required electrical cardioversion or external defibrillation.

3.4. Clinical Prognosis Two patients (1.9%) died during hospitalization. After discharge, 30-day mortality was 4.9% and 1-year mortality reached 17.2%. Patients deceased within one year were older (median age was 74 vs. 70 years, p < 0.05). Patients with idiopathic VT had a better prognosis when compared with those with structural heart disease, in terms of both 1-year mortality (11% vs. 17%; p < 0.05), reaching the clinical endpoint (20% vs. 27%; p < 0.05), and the arrhythmic endpoint (30% vs. 35%; p < 0.05). As reported in Figure 5 , Kaplan–Meier analysis showed a 64% survival at 1000 days after discharge, decreasing to 45% at 2400 days.
Ejection fraction ≤ 30%, even after adjusting for age, was strongly associated with 1-year mortality (OR 10.158; p = 0.003) as well as age-adjusted serum creatinine (OR 2.45; p = 0.048).

Patients who experienced arrhythmic recurrence during hospitalization had a 7.42-fold higher risk of death ( p = 0.028) within 1 year after discharge compared with those without in-hospital arrhythmic recurrences. In multivariable analysis, arrhythmic recurrence during hospitalization showed the strongest association with 1-year mortality, regardless of a prior history of cardiomyopathy. Indeed, the distribution of ischemic cardiomyopathy and other structural heart diseases reflected that of the overall study population (91% with structural cardiomyopathy, 59% of whom had an ischemic etiology). To reduce the risk of overfitting, we also revised the primary multivariable analysis by restricting the model to a smaller number of clinically prespecified covariates. Specifically, we tested Model A: in-hospital arrhythmic recurrence and age, and Model B: in-hospital arrhythmic recurrence and LVEF ≤ 30%. In Model A, arrhythmic recurrence remained better associated with one-year mortality (OR 3.925; p = 0.020). Similarly, in Model B, arrhythmic recurrence remained superior, associated with one-year mortality (OR 4.20; p = 0.028).

4. Discussion The present study provides three main findings. First, ischemic heart disease remained the predominant substrate for sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT). Second, acute management in the Emergency Department (ED) frequently diverged from contemporary guideline-recommended pathways. Third, advanced age, severely impaired left ventricular systolic function (LVEF < 30%), elevated serum creatinine, and in-hospital arrhythmic recurrence were independently associated with an increased risk of one-year mortality. Notably, arrhythmic recurrence during the index hospitalization was the most powerful predictor in the multivariable analysis.

Although limited in absolute terms, our sample size compares favorably with those of several previously published single-center studies of sustained VT, supporting the clinical relevance of this real-world ED cohort [ 7 , 8 , 9 ]. Our cohort (n = 103) consisted predominantly of elderly, male, and overweight patients, with structural heart disease documented in approximately 90% of cases, most commonly of ischemic etiology. Compared with earlier series, our patients were older and more frequently male, a difference that may reflect demographic changes, improved survival after cardiovascular events, and the increasing complexity of patients presenting to the ED. Idiopathic VT was observed more frequently than in previous reports and, as expected, was associated with more favorable outcomes, consistent with the available literature [ 4 , 10 , 11 , 12 ]. The prevalence of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was substantially lower than that reported by Domanovits et al. [ 7 ], in whom AMI was diagnosed in nearly one-third of VT presentations. This discrepancy may be partly explained by our case-identification strategy, which relied on the ICD-9-CM code for paroxysmal VT and may therefore have excluded patients whose primary discharge diagnosis was acute coronary syndrome. Because patient identification relied solely on ICD-9-CM code 427.1, our study may have underestimated the true number of sustained VT presentations by excluding cases coded primarily as acute myocardial infarction or cardiac arrest. This selection strategy limits generalizability to the full spectrum of VT presentations but focuses the analysis on patients in whom sustained VT represented the main acute clinical problem and for whom antiarrhythmic management and rhythm-control strategies were central to ED decision-making. This selection bias may have partially contributed to the more favorable prognosis observed in our cohort.

Median LVEF values (35% historically, 30% during hospitalization) confirmed a population with markedly impaired cardiac function. A substantial proportion of patients had an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), often presenting due to device shocks or arrhythmic recurrences, while prior catheter ablation was uncommon. Chest pain was the most frequently reported symptom, followed by palpitations, consistent with the study conducted by Havakuk et al. [ 12 ] and descriptions in major internal medicine and cardiology textbooks [ 13 ].

Acute treatment patterns revealed a clinically meaningful gap between evidence and practice. Adenosine was administered in nine patients with regular monomorphic, hemodynamically stable VT, in accordance with ACLS guidelines, to evaluate wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin and exclude supraventricular tachycardia [ 4 , 14 , 15 ]. In patients with hemodynamically tolerated VT, pharmacological therapy—most commonly amiodarone—represented the predominant first-line strategy. This may reflect its widespread availability, familiarity among emergency clinicians, and perceived short-term safety. However, intravenous procainamide was not used in the ED and was administered only rarely during hospitalization. Despite growing evidence supporting procainamide as the most effective antiarrhythmic for stable monomorphic VT, continued use of lidocaine further suggests a discrepancy between contemporary evidence and real-world prescribing patterns [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ]. Studies evaluating procainamide, lidocaine, amiodarone and sotalol are still limited and nevertheless, the strength of the evidence base remains vitiated by the small number of trials, heterogeneity in patient populations and eligibility criteria, and differences in outcome definitions [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ]. The absence of procainamide use in the ED may have reflected not only clinical inertia or greater familiarity with amiodarone, but also practical factors such as its inclusion in the standard ED formulary and the availability of staff specifically trained in its administration and monitoring. In spite of guideline recommendations, even electrical cardioversion (ECV) was underutilized in stable patients and not consistently applied as first-line therapy in unstable cases, where it remains the recommended strategy. Although anesthetic risk may have influenced decision-making, pharmacological treatment should not delay electrical cardioversion in unstable patients and may itself cause hypotension or arrhythmic events. However, this result should be interpreted in light of the study period, as more than half of patients were enrolled before publication of the most recent ESC guideline update in 2022 [ 4 ].

Beyond individual clinician preference, organizational factors may contribute to this evidence–practice gap. Although electrical cardioversion is an established and highly effective intervention, its prompt delivery may depend on the immediate availability of trained staff, appropriate monitoring, resuscitation equipment, and procedural sedation and analgesia. Even ED overcrowding can play a role. In real-world ED practice, limitations in these resources may influence treatment selection and reduce adherence to guideline-recommended pathways. The increasing availability of emergency physicians with formal training and experience in procedural sedation and invasive bedside procedures may facilitate wider implementation of ECV. Concurrently, the use of regional anesthesia and peripheral nerve blocks in emergency medicine is expanding beyond analgesia for multiple rib fractures, with growing application across a range of procedures [ 5 , 21 ]. This evolving expertise may also support the future integration of autonomic modulation techniques, including stellate ganglion block, as rescue or bridging strategies in selected patients with refractory ventricular arrhythmias or electrical storm. Notably, eight patients in our cohort underwent stellate ganglion block during hospitalization: the procedure was used early in the treatment course in one patient and as rescue therapy in the remaining seven patients. Although our study was not designed to assess its efficacy, this experience reflects the increasing incorporation of stellate ganglion block into the multidisciplinary management of highly selected patients with refractory ventricular arrhythmias.

Prognostic analysis confirmed the central role of baseline cardiac and systemic disease severity. An LVEF ≤ 30% was strongly associated with one-year mortality, conferring a more than ninefold increase in the risk of death. This result is consistent with previous studies identifying severe left ventricular dysfunction as a major prognostic marker and as a key criterion for primary-prevention ICD implantation in patients at risk of ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Elevated serum creatinine was also moderately associated with mortality, likely reflecting the contribution of renal dysfunction, cardiorenal disease, and overall clinical complexity. Most importantly, in-hospital VT recurrence was associated with a 6.4-fold increase in one-year mortality. This observation identifies early arrhythmic instability as a clinically relevant marker of adverse prognosis and supports the need for prompt recognition of high-risk patients, early optimization of antiarrhythmic and hemodynamic management, and timely referral for advanced electrophysiological assessment when appropriate.

5. Limitations This study has several limitations. First, it was conducted retrospectively in a single Emergency Department of a tertiary-care IRCCS Hospital. This may limit the generalizability of our findings. Our cohort likely reflects a referral population with greater baseline cardiac complexity, including a higher burden of structural heart disease, severe left ventricular dysfunction, ICD carriers, and recurrent ventricular arrhythmias than would be expected in community EDs. Furthermore, the design may have introduced selection bias, particularly in the identification of VT cases based on administrative coding ICD-9. Finally, the cause of death was not systematically recorded, limiting further analysis of mortality outcomes.

6. Conclusions In this real-world ED cohort, sustained VT with a pulse was an uncommon but high-risk presentation, occurring predominantly in patients with structural heart disease of ischemic origin. Acute management frequently diverged from guideline-recommended care. One-year mortality was substantial and was independently associated with severely reduced left ventricular systolic function and, most strongly, with in-hospital arrhythmic recurrence. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to clarify its prognostic value and assess whether improved guideline adherence can enhance patient outcomes.

Abstract Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) arise from an early depolarization originating in either of the cardiac ventricles. They are common in individuals both with and without structural heart disease, although their true prevalence remains uncertain. Several electrophysiological mechanisms can initiate the PVC, with re-entry being the most frequent. The detection of PVCs should prompt a thorough clinical evaluation to identify potential underlying cardiac disease, yet many PVCs ultimately prove to be idiopathic. In individuals with established structural heart disease, PVCs have been associated with a poorer prognosis; however, clinical trials aimed at suppressing PVCs in this population have not demonstrated improved outcomes. In contrast, the prognostic significance of PVCs in patients without structural heart disease remains unclear. Factors such as PVC burden, PVC morphology, and cardiac magnetic resonance findings have been proposed as prognostic markers, although the evidence is still debated. In general, patients without structural heart disease and with a low PVC burden can be reassured regarding their prognosis. Treatment is primarily guided by symptoms, although reducing PVC burden may be considered even in asymptomatic individuals to mitigate the risk of complications such as PVC-induced cardiomyopathy or PVC-triggered sustained ventricular arrhythmias. Antiarrhythmic drugs are commonly used as first-line therapy, and the choice of medication should take into account patient characteristics, suspected pathophysiology, and PVC features. Catheter ablation (CA) is more effective than pharmacologic therapy in reducing or eliminating PVCs and may be considered as a first-line option in specific situations where rapid PVC suppression is desired. As an invasive procedure, CA carries potential risks that must be weighed carefully. Operator experience, PVC origin, anatomical considerations, and patient preference all play important roles in decision-making. Further research is needed to better identify patients at risk and to target specific pathophysiological mechanisms. Advances in device-based, patient-driven arrhythmia monitoring and the integration of artificial intelligence are likely to influence future PVC diagnostics and risk stratification.

They were described already in the 18th century 1 and are most commonly identified on a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), appearing as a widened QRS complex (typically >120 milliseconds) that occurs earlier than the expected normal complex and without a preceding P wave. PVCs are generally followed by a compensatory pause and are associated with a discordant ST-T segment. The site of origin can be inferred from the morphology on the 12-lead ECG, while PVCs may be further classified according to frequency (expressed as absolute counts or percentage of total beats/PVC burden), coupling interval, QRS duration, and complexity (unifocal, multifocal, couplets, triplets). Alternative terminology includes premature ventricular beats, premature ventricular depolarizations, premature ventricular contractions, ventricular ectopic activity, ventricular ectopic beats, ventricular premature depolarizations, and ventricular extrasystoles. Nevertheless, the 2019 HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS consensus statement on catheter ablation of ventricular arrhythmias consistently uses the term premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) , and this terminology has subsequently been widely adopted in the literature. 2 This terminology emphasizes that the electrical activity of a PVC does not invariably result in a mechanical ventricular contraction.

PVCs are frequently encountered in clinical practice and may occur in individuals both with and without structural heart disease (SHD). 3 In patients without evidence of structural or inherited cardiac pathology, PVCs are classified as idiopathic. The predominant source of idiopathic PVCs is the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) 4 with left ventricular outflow tract and intracavitary ventricular structures following in frequency. Other sites of origin, such as the valvular annular regions, the left bundle fascicles or epicardial foci, are more uncommon. 5 PVCs may be entirely asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, or they may manifest with symptoms that range from bothersome to debilitating, such as palpitations—often perceived as chest discomfort, irregular heartbeats, or the sensation of a missed beat—along with dizziness, dyspnoea, or fatigue. 6 Determining whether PVCs in patients without SHD are truly idiopathic, and whether they influence prognosis, is of considerable clinical importance, as it directly informs decisions regarding diagnostic evaluation, follow-up, and therapeutic strategies.

Epidemiology Numerous studies have investigated the PVC prevalence in the general population, employing diverse inclusion criteria and varying approaches to electrocardiographic recording, which has resulted in markedly heterogeneous findings. One of the earliest large-scale ECG-based epidemiological investigations was conducted in 1962, when Roland Hiss and Lawrence Lamb examined approximately 120 000 apparently healthy males and reported that nearly 5% exhibited electrocardiographic anomalies, with 7.8 per 1000 demonstrating PVCs. 7 Data from the ARIC study indicate a PVC prevalence of about 5%, rising to 23% among subjects with hypertension. 8 Fisher reported an incidence of about 7%, 9 Kennedy et al. estimated a prevalence of 1–4% in the general population, 10 while Kostis et al . reported a prevalence approaching 40%. 11 The MRFIT study, 12 based on a large cohort, reported a prevalence of 4%, while Yang et al ., in another large cohort undergoing Holter monitoring, found that 1.3% of the patients had a very high burden of PVCs (≥20% of total heartbeats). 13 More recently, patch-based ECG has enabled extended recording periods, and screening of an elderly population revealed that 99.5% experienced at least one isolated PVC per hour, with 34.6% demonstrating ventricular tachycardia (defined as more than four consecutive ventricular beats) over a 24-hour period. 14 Some major studies investigating PVC prevalence in population-based cohorts or healthy individuals are summarized in Table 1 .

Pathophysiology Three principal mechanisms have been implicated in the genesis of ectopic beats: re-entry, increased automaticity, and triggered activity. For a re-entry phenomenon to occur, two distinct electrical pathways must be present, with one pathway exhibiting unidirectional block. These pathways provide the substrate for arrhythmogenesis and may involve either established anatomical structures (e.g. bundle branches, fascicles) or regions with altered conduction velocity resulting from pathological processes in cardiac tissue. A classic example is the fibrotic scar produced by myocardial infarction or myocarditis. When a depolarization wave traverses such a fibrotic area, conduction may be sufficiently delayed to reach adjacent healthy myocardium that is no longer refractory, thereby initiating one or more ectopic beats. This mechanism helps explain the higher prevalence of PVCs in populations with increased cardiovascular risk, including males, smokers, the elderly, and individuals with hypertension or impaired ventricular function. 8 , 15 , 16 Triggered activity occurs when excessive calcium influx elevates intracellular concentrations, leading to spontaneous calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and subsequent delayed afterdepolarization. However, the precise mechanisms by which this process generates focal electrical activity remain incompletely understood. 17 Prolonged repolarization and delayed afterdepolarization are observed under conditions such as bradycardia, digitalis intoxication, hypokalaemia, and Long QT syndrome. 18–20 Enhanced electrical automaticity—defined as the intrinsic ability of myocardial cells to depolarize spontaneously and initiate new depolarization waves—may also contribute to PVC formation. This mechanism is multifactorial, encompassing catecholaminergic stimulation, transient or permanent tissue alterations, and inherent cellular properties. 21 , 22 Although these mechanisms may seem primarily of academic interest, understanding the biological basis of PVCs is clinically significant, as it represents a key determinant of therapeutic success. 23

The role of mitral valve prolapse (MVP) in PVC pathophysiology deserves a special mention. Up to 1–3% of people have MVP, and this condition carries a connection to PVCs, which are seen in about 40–50% of affected individuals 24 The underlying mechanism is thought to involve the prolapsing valve leaflet physically tugging on the papillary muscles; this mechanical stress can activate stretch-sensitive afterdepolarizations and trigger abnormal automaticity in the distal Purkinje network. 25 Adding to this, heightened sympathetic activity observed in some of these patients tends to worsen the degree of ventricular ectopy. For the most part, PVCs linked to MVP carry a benign prognosis. However, when these ectopic beats become complex or pleomorphic, particularly if they originate from Purkinje tissue, they can potentially set off ventricular fibrillation and lead to sudden cardiac death. This risk climbs notably in patients who also show bileaflet prolapse, mitral annular disjunction, or fibrotic changes in the myocardium detected via cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR). 26

Diagnostic workup Frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) are strongly associated with a range of comorbid conditions; therefore, clinical evaluation should primarily focus on identifying or excluding underlying cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular disease. A comprehensive medical history is indispensable, encompassing presenting symptoms, precipitating factors, established cardiac pathology, cardiovascular risk profiles, current pharmacotherapy, prior medical conditions, and relevant family history. In addition to a standard physical examination, diagnostic assessment should include a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) to delineate PVC morphology and to detect potential markers of concomitant cardiac or electrolyte disturbances. Laboratory investigations should evaluate serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, and calcium), renal function, and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels. For patients whose symptoms are exercise-induced, an exercise stress test is indicated. Furthermore, ambulatory ECG monitoring should be utilized to quantify PVC burden and to establish correlations between arrhythmic events and patient-reported symptoms. 27 , 28 Echocardiography is widely recognized as the first-line imaging modality, providing critical information on cardiac function and the detection of potential structural abnormalities. 27 , 29 Clinical evaluation should also encompass the exclusion of underlying coronary artery disease, guided by the patient’s estimated pretest probability. When SHD other than coronary artery disease is suspected based on initial findings, CMR should be considered as a complementary diagnostic tool. 28 , 29 In recent years, the role of CMR has been increasingly emphasized, particularly given that the detection of fibrosis by CMR has been associated with poorer prognostic outcomes in this patient population. 30 Given that CMR is a resource-intensive examination, efforts have been made to delineate and standardize its indications in patients with premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). 31 A suggested diagnostic work-up is described in Figure 1 . 7–9 , 11 , 12

Prognostic impact—historic perspective of the evidence In 1985, Kennedy s . published a study of 73 asymptomatic, healthy individuals with frequent and complex ventricular ectopy who had been followed for 10 years, demonstrating prognoses comparable to those of the general population. 10 These findings were confirmed in a subsequent study by the same author 32 underscoring the continued interest in clarifying the prognostic implications of PVCs in healthy subjects. 33 Numerous studies published throughout the 1980s and 1990s produced conflicting results. A common criticism of these investigations was the insufficient application of rigorous diagnostic methods to exclude underlying cardiac disease. 34 In 1992, Kostis summarized the available evidence, concluding that PVCs do not independently contribute to mortality but may instead serve as markers of occult heart disease. 33 The adverse prognostic impact of PVCs is more evident in the presence of structural heart disease. Findings from studies conducted in the 1960s and 1970s were corroborated in subsequent decades, particularly among patients with prior ischaemic events. 35–38 Even in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, a relationship between PVCs and poor outcomes has been established. 39 , 40 In a 1993 review, 41 Myerburg et al . emphasized the role of PVCs in the pathophysiology of malignant arrhythmias, identifying them as the link between ischaemia and ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation. Meanwhile, the CAST trial demonstrated that suppression of ventricular ectopy with class I antiarrhythmic drugs in myocardial infarction survivors did not improve prognosis; on the contrary, patients treated with flecainide or encainide experienced higher mortality compared to those receiving placebo. 42 These findings reinforced the conclusion that PVCs are not independent contributors to mortality but rather markers of underlying disease. While the prognostic impact of PVCs in structural heart disease appears indisputable, evidence regarding their role in healthy individuals remains uncertain. Many studies reporting a negative impact relied solely on patient history to exclude structural disease and/or were conducted exclusively in male populations 12 , 43–48 . Among large population studies, Agarwal 49 demonstrated a higher incidence of heart failure (HF) in PVC patients compared with controls. Notably, the association between PVCs and incident HF was strongest in patients with fewer cardiovascular risk factors, with a six-fold increase in risk among those younger than 65 years without CHD, diabetes, hypertension, or atrial fibrillation. In a 12-year follow-up of Japanese men and women, 50 Hirose reported increased cardiovascular mortality among men with PVCs, whereas no prognostic impact was observed in women. More recent studies in Asian populations have again shown associations between PVCs and all-cause mortality, hospitalization, and HF at the population level. 48 , 51 Among the studies that incorporated echocardiographic evaluation at baseline, Dukes et al . 52 examined 1139 individuals whose PVC frequency was quantified by Holter monitoring. They found that individuals in the highest quartile of PVC frequency had a threefold risk of a five-year decline in LVEF, a 48% increased risk of incident CHF, and a 31% increased risk of death compared to those in the lowest quartile, after adjustment for confounders and a median follow-up of 13 years. Results were similar when PVCs were analysed as a continuous variable. In contrast, Lee et al 53 reported that only a small proportion of PVC patients with normal LVEF developed systolic dysfunction during approximately 5 years of follow-up.

Alongside studies demonstrating a negative prognostic impact of PVCs in the general population or in cohorts without apparent heart disease, others found no such association. Fisher 9 reported that the risk of coronary artery disease was not increased by the presence of PVCs on routine ECG in a cohort of factory workers aged 35–69. A decade later, Kennedy et al 10 published results from a 6.5-year follow-up of 73 asymptomatic, healthy subjects with frequent ventricular ectopy, reporting only one case of sudden death. Compared to the standardized mortality ratio, this suggested that long-term prognosis was not adversely affected by PVCs. This study contributed significantly to the view that PVCs are benign in the absence of structural heart disease, and several subsequent publications appear to confirm its findings. 53–58 In a study specifically focused on the potential development of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), Gaita et al 59 followed 61 patients with frequent right-ventricular PVCs. After an average follow-up of 15 years, no patient had died of SCD or developed ARVC, and half no longer exhibited PVCs. In a cohort of 5000 athletes, Verdile et al 60 observed that exercise-induced PVCs tended to resolve spontaneously or could be successfully treated, without affecting clinical outcomes.

Although studies reporting a negative prognostic impact of PVCs in subjects without apparent heart disease outnumber those showing no association, the overall evidence remains divided and inconclusive. This uncertainty is compounded by the fact that few studies consistently employed imaging diagnostics to exclude structural disease, relying instead on patient history. Meta-analyses addressing this issue were lacking until 2012, when Lee et al 61 published the first, followed shortly by Ataklte and colleagues. 62 Lee’s meta-analysis included studies with control populations based on adults without apparent heart disease, excluding unselected populations not evaluated for structural disease, studies of exercise-induced PVCs, and subgroup analyses within PVC cohorts. When multiple studies were based on the same cohort, only the most recent was included. Out of more than 3000 studies published between 1966 and 2011, only eight met these criteria, all of which were prospective observational cohort studies. Sensitivity analysis revealed that negative prognostic effects were observed primarily in male-only cohorts, while the single study incorporating echocardiography and exercise testing at baseline did not demonstrate worsened outcomes. According to the authors, heterogeneity among studies was substantial, and publication bias was not apparent. The pooled OR for death, cardiovascular death, SCD, or ischaemic heart disease was 1.72 (95% CI 1.28–2.31). Classic cardiovascular risk factors such as male gender, age, diabetes, and hypertension increased the odds of cardiovascular events, suggesting that patients with undetected structural disease were included, thereby influencing results. The authors concluded that if more advanced diagnostic techniques had been used to exclude structural disease, benign outcomes with PVCs would likely have been observed. Consistent with this, study quality assessment indicated that the increase in OR was less pronounced in higher-quality studies. Ataklte et al . included prospective cohort, nested case-control, and retrospective cohort studies, ultimately analysing 11 relevant investigations involving 106 000 patients. The prevalence of PVCs ranged from 1.2% to 10.7%, with mean follow-up times of 5–30 years. The six prospective studies showed no significant heterogeneity. The pooled RR for total cardiac death was 2.1 and the authors proposed two hypotheses: PVCs may trigger fatal ventricular arrhythmias, or they may represent markers of underlying disease (reverse causation). They also noted insufficient adjustment for confounders in some studies, though they did not emphasize the lack of diagnostic imaging as strongly as Lee et al.

More recent publications have continued to present conflicting evidence, with some studies suggesting a benign clinical course, 53 , 57 , 58 whereas others indicate a negative prognostic impact. 48 , 63 Two review articles recommend that patients with a low PVC burden and normal echocardiographic findings may be reassured, while those with a potentially significant burden or deemed at risk for cardiomyopathy should undergo regular clinical follow-up. 64 , 65 In a Japanese study based on retrospective data from an administrative database, 66 the frequency of PVCs, based on Holter monitoring, was not associated with clinical events, while the presence of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia was independently associated to heart failure incidence. A recent third meta-analysis, encompassing 25 studies, examined the relationship between PVCs and cardiovascular outcomes in populations without overt structural heart disease. 67 The analysis demonstrated that frequent PVCs were significantly associated with an increased risk of mortality, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and stroke. However, the authors emphasized that, according to the GRADE framework, the overall quality of evidence was rated as low. This assessment was primarily attributed to the observational nature of the included studies and methodological limitations, such as incomplete adjustment for clinically relevant confounders related to underlying heart disease. Additionally, concerns regarding residual confounding and selection bias, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings, were highlighted as further limitations. Some of the more recent studies investigating the prognostic impact of PVCs in healthy or apparently healthy subjects are summarized in Table 2 .
